fields.summary: A small woodland hawk with short, rounded wings and a long tail. It is an agile hunter that catches other birds.
fields.size: 28 to 38 cm long, wingspan 58 to 75 cm, 105 to 350 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts with fast, surprise flights through hedges and trees. It mostly catches small birds like sparrows or tits. The female is much bigger than the male and can even catch a pigeon-sized bird.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods, hedgerows, parks and gardens. It likes to hunt near bird feeders, where small birds gather.
fields.migration: In France, some stay all year, while others fly short distances. In winter, birds from northern Europe come to join them.
fields.enemies: The Northern Goshawk, which is bigger, can catch it.
fields.by_ear: It is fairly quiet outside the breeding season. Then it gives a sharp, repeated, fast « ki-ki-ki-ki », mostly near the nest.
fields.confusions: The Common Kestrel has pointed wings and hovers in place. The Eurasian Sparrowhawk has short, rounded wings and never hangs still in the air.
fields.anecdote: In the Eurasian Sparrowhawk, the female is much bigger and heavier than the male. It is one of the biggest size gaps between the sexes among European birds of prey.
fields.hint: The female is much bigger than the male.

fields.summary: A small, streaky brown bird of wet places. You can spot it by the clear cream-white stripe above its eye.
fields.size: 13 cm long, wingspan 17 to 21 cm, 10 to 15 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects in the low plants of marshes. It often sings during a short flight above the rushes.
fields.why_here: It lives in marshes, reedbeds and wet places with low, thick plants, rushes and sedges.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara as early as August or September.
fields.by_ear: A very varied, fast song, a mix of trills and copies of other birds. It is often sung in a song flight.
fields.confusions: It is often mixed up with the Common Reed Warbler. The Sedge Warbler has a clear stripe over the eye and a streaky back, which tell them apart.
fields.anecdote: The Sedge Warbler sometimes sings as it rises briefly above the reeds, then drops back down to land.
fields.hint: A pale stripe above my eye, I sing among the rushes.

fields.summary: A small, plain brown bird of reedbeds. It is hard to see but very chatty, and typical of pond edges.
fields.size: 12.5 to 13 cm long, wingspan 17 to 21 cm, 10 to 15 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects caught among the reeds. It sings nonstop from the stems, often hidden in thick plants.
fields.why_here: It lives in thick reedbeds at the edge of ponds, rivers and marshes. There it builds a woven nest between the stems.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.enemies: The Western Marsh Harrier can raid its nest or catch the adults.
fields.by_ear: A rhythmic, repeating song of creaky, croaking phrases, repeated like « tirr-tirr-tchourr-tchourr » for long minutes.
fields.confusions: It is often mixed up with other water warblers like the Sedge Warbler, which has a clear stripe over the eye and a more varied song.
fields.anecdote: The Common Reed Warbler is one of the Common Cuckoo's favourite hosts. The cuckoo often lays its eggs in its woven nest between the reeds.
fields.hint: Hidden by the pond, I repeat the same notes again and again.

fields.summary: A tiny bird with a very long tail and soft black, white and pink feathers. It always travels in small flocks.
fields.size: 13 to 15 cm long, half of it tail, wingspan 16 to 19 cm, 7 to 9 g
fields.behaviour: It travels in groups of ten to twenty that go from tree to tree together, calling all the time. It looks for tiny insects and spiders on thin branches.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedges, thickets and woodland edges with thorny bushes. There it weaves a round nest of moss and spider webs that stretches while the chicks grow.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year. The family group remains together in a fairly small area.
fields.enemies: Jays and crows can raid its nest. Small birds of prey can also hunt the adults.
fields.by_ear: Nonstop calls in flight: a string of small, sharp « tsi-tsi-tsi » mixed with a rolling « tsrrr ». They give the flock away before you even see it.
fields.confusions: Its round shape with a huge tail makes it unique. No other tit in France has a tail this long compared to its body.
fields.anecdote: Its nest is a ball of moss and lichen lined with feathers. It can hold over a thousand feathers and stretches like elastic as the chicks grow.
fields.hint: I travel in noisy little groups from tree to tree.

fields.summary: A streaky brown bird of farmland, famous for its endless song sung very high up.
fields.size: 18 to 19 cm long, wingspan 30 to 36 cm, 30 to 45 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects on the ground in fields. It climbs straight up while singing, sometimes until it disappears from view.
fields.why_here: It lives in big farming plains, crops and open meadows, where it nests right on the ground.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Birds from the north and east spend the winter here, which adds to the numbers from October to March.
fields.enemies: The Hen Harrier, the Carrion Crow and the Red Fox can attack its nests and chicks.
fields.by_ear: A nonstop, rich, flute-like song sung while hovering very high, sometimes for several minutes without a break.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Crested Lark, which is stockier, has a pointed crest and does not sing in long, steep flights.
fields.anecdote: The Eurasian Skylark can sing in flight for more than five minutes in a row, sometimes climbing out of sight of the naked eye.
fields.hint: I climb higher and higher and sing without stopping.

fields.summary: A small, brightly coloured bird with a turquoise-blue back and an orange belly. It dives like an arrow to catch fish.
fields.size: 16 to 17 cm long, wingspan 24 to 26 cm, 34 to 46 g
fields.behaviour: It watches for small fish from a perch above the water, then dives suddenly to catch them. It stuns them by hitting them on its perch.
fields.why_here: It lives by calm streams, ponds and rivers with soft banks, where it digs a burrow to nest.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. In hard winters, frozen water can push it south or toward the coast.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, whistling « tsiii » called in fast, straight flight just above the water.
fields.confusions: Few birds in Europe can be mixed up with it thanks to its unique colours. Its fast, low flight can make it easy to miss.
fields.anecdote: The Common Kingfisher digs a burrow more than half a metre long into a soft bank to lay its eggs.
fields.hint: Blue and orange, I dive like an arrow into the water.

fields.summary: The most common duck in Europe. The male has a bright green head. The female is brown and speckled, and harder to notice.
fields.size: 50 to 65 cm long, wingspan 81 to 98 cm, 850 to 1400 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds on the surface or by tipping its head under the water, which is called dabbling. It eats water plants, seeds and small animals without backbones.
fields.why_here: It lives at almost every kind of water: ponds, rivers and city parks, where it finds food and peace to raise its young.
fields.migration: Most stay in France all year. In winter, birds from northern Europe join them.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox, the martens and the Eurasian Otter are among its predators.
fields.by_ear: The female gives the well-known loud « quack-quack ». The male makes only a softer, hoarse whistle.
fields.confusions: The male is hard to mix up. The brown female can look like other dabbling ducks, such as the Gadwall.
fields.anecdote: Only the female Mallard quacks loudly. Despite what many people think, the male makes just a soft whistle.
fields.hint: Only the female quacks loudly. The male just whistles.

fields.summary: A small, streaky brown bird that is easy to overlook. It is typical of moors and open meadows, and often mixed up with other pipits.
fields.size: 14.5 cm long, wingspan 22 to 25 cm, 15 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects and small seeds on the ground. It does a typical song flight, then floats down like a parachute.
fields.why_here: It lives on moors, wet meadows, marshes and open coastal areas with few trees.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Birds from northern Europe come to spend the winter in France, from October to March.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox can raid its nest on the ground.
fields.by_ear: A thin, sharp « ist-ist-ist » call, repeated. The song is given in flight and ends with a gliding drop.
fields.confusions: It is often mixed up with the Tree Pipit, which lives more in trees, has a rougher call and a different song flight.
fields.anecdote: The Meadow Pipit is the Common Cuckoo's most frequent host. The cuckoo often lays its eggs in its nest.
fields.hint: Quiet and streaky brown, I sing as I fall from the sky.

fields.summary: A streaky brown songbird close to the Meadow Pipit, but it sticks more to woodland edges and happily perches in trees.
fields.size: 15 cm long, wingspan 25 to 27 cm, 20 to 25 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects on the ground. It sings in flight from a tree, rising up and then floating back down like a parachute to where it started.
fields.why_here: It lives at the edges of light woods, in clearings and in farmland with scattered trees for singing and perching.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Hobby can hunt it. The Eurasian Sparrowhawk catches it more rarely.
fields.by_ear: A loud, varied song that ends with a typical drawn-out « sia-sia-sia » as the bird floats down.
fields.confusions: It is often mixed up with the Meadow Pipit, but the Tree Pipit perches in trees and its song ends differently.
fields.anecdote: The Tree Pipit always starts its song flight from a perch. The Meadow Pipit, by contrast, takes off from the ground.
fields.hint: I leave a branch to sing, then glide back to it.

fields.summary: An all-black bird with thin, sickle-shaped wings. It spends almost its whole life in the air, even sleeping there.
fields.size: 16 to 17 cm long, wingspan 42 to 48 cm, 36 to 50 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects very high in the sky, and drinks and eats on the wing. It never lands on the ground on purpose, because its legs are too short.
fields.why_here: It lives in towns and villages. It nests in holes in old buildings, under roofs, or in nest boxes made for it.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in late April or May and leaves as early as late July or early August. It is one of the first migrants to leave Europe.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Hobby can catch this bird in flight.
fields.by_ear: A shrill, piercing scream, a high whistle given in flight during noisy group chases around houses.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with swallows, but the Common Swift has longer, narrower, sickle-shaped wings and a faster, stiffer flight.
fields.anecdote: The Common Swift can stay in the air for several months without landing, eating and even sleeping on the wing.
fields.hint: I almost never land, not even to sleep.

fields.summary: A tall, slim grey wading bird with a long neck and a long, pointed beak. It stands still for long minutes while hunting.
fields.size: 90 to 98 cm long, wingspan 175 to 195 cm, 1 to 2 kg
fields.behaviour: It waits without moving, or walks slowly in shallow water. With a quick stab of its beak, it catches fish, frogs and small animals.
fields.why_here: It lives at the edge of ponds, rivers and marshes full of fish. It nests in colonies in tall trees.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Others move south in winter when the water freezes.
fields.by_ear: A deep, hoarse call, a loud croak « krannk » given mostly when taking off or flying.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Little Egret, which is all white, or the White Stork, which flies with its beak straight and its neck stretched out, not folded.
fields.anecdote: The Grey Heron can stay still for over an hour, like a grey statue by the water, before striking its prey in a flash.
fields.hint: Standing still by the water, I strike in a flash.

fields.summary: A slim owl with long, easy-to-see feather tufts and bright orange eyes. It often sits upright and still against a conifer trunk.
fields.size: 35 to 37 cm long, wingspan 90 to 100 cm, 190 to 435 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts at night over open fields and meadows, eating mostly small rodents like voles. In winter, it often roosts in groups, called roosts, in the same conifer.
fields.why_here: It lives at woodland edges and in conifer groves close to open farmland where it hunts. It often reuses old crow nests instead of building its own.
fields.migration: Some migrate in France. Some stay all year, others move in winter, sometimes joined by birds from northern Europe.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can catch the Long-eared Owl.
fields.by_ear: A deep, soft song, a low « hoo » repeated at regular, spaced intervals. It is much quieter than the hooting of the Tawny Owl.
fields.confusions: Its long, easy-to-see feather tufts and orange eyes set it apart from the Tawny Owl, which has dark eyes and no tufts.
fields.anecdote: In winter, several Long-eared Owls can gather to roost in one tree, sometimes in the middle of a town. People who find them are often surprised.
fields.hint: Feathery tufts rise above my bright orange eyes.

fields.summary: A small, stocky owl with big yellow eyes. It is also active by day and often perches in plain view on a post or an old wall.
fields.size: 21 to 23 cm long, wingspan 54 to 58 cm, 150 to 200 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts mostly insects, earthworms and small rodents, often at the end of the day but also in full daylight. It bobs its head and body up and down when disturbed.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedgerow farmland, old fruit orchards and old country buildings. There it finds holes to nest in, especially in old walls and hollow trees.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, on the same small territory around its nest site.
fields.enemies: The Beech Marten can raid its nest. The Eurasian Magpie can take eggs or chicks from it.
fields.by_ear: A clear, flute-like call, a single-syllable « kiew » repeated, and a softer song in spring.
fields.confusions: It is much smaller than the Tawny Owl. It also has more daytime habits and often perches in plain view in daylight.
fields.anecdote: It is linked to the Greek goddess Athena as a symbol of wisdom. It is one of the few owls you can easily see in daylight, sitting still in the sun.
fields.hint: You can often spot me in daylight, sitting still.

fields.summary: The most common daytime bird of prey in France. It has a stocky shape with broad wings, and its feathers vary a lot, from dark brown to almost white.
fields.size: 51 to 57 cm long, wingspan 113 to 128 cm, 550 to 1300 g
fields.behaviour: It mostly hunts small rodents like voles, often waiting on a pole or gliding in circles in the sky. Sometimes it also eats dead animals.
fields.why_here: It lives in countryside, woods, hedgerow farmland and edges almost everywhere in France. It needs trees to nest in and open spaces to hunt.
fields.migration: Most stay in France all year. Buzzards from northern Europe fly through the country or spend the winter here.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can catch the Common Buzzard.
fields.by_ear: A typical call, a sad, piercing mew, often given while gliding. It sounds a bit like a cat calling in the sky.
fields.confusions: The very varied colours can be mixed up with other birds of prey. But its stocky shape, broad rounded wings and mewing call are good clues.
fields.anecdote: Its colours differ so much from bird to bird, from very dark brown to almost white, that two Common Buzzards can look like different species.
fields.hint: My cry sounds like a mew thrown into the sky.

fields.summary: A small, very colourful finch with a bright red face mask and black wings crossed by a bright yellow band. It is one of the easiest garden birds to recognise.
fields.size: 12 to 13.5 cm long, wingspan 21 to 25.5 cm, 14 to 19 g
fields.behaviour: It eats mostly small seeds, especially thistle and dandelion seeds, picked out with its thin, pointed beak. It is sociable and forms groups called « charms » outside the breeding season.
fields.why_here: It likes wasteland, flowery gardens, orchards and path edges where thistles and other seed plants grow. It nests high in a tree, often at the end of a thin branch.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Some French goldfinches stay put, while others fly to southern Europe for winter and are replaced by birds from the north.
fields.enemies: The house cat can catch the European Goldfinch.
fields.by_ear: A light, twittering song, a string of crystal-clear notes and little trills, often sung in flight or perched in a group. Its contact call is a light, musical « tsi-tsi-witt ».
fields.confusions: Its red mask and yellow and black wings are unique among garden birds. There is little risk of mix-up once you see an adult's feathers well.
fields.anecdote: A group of goldfinches is called a « charm », because of their light, harmonious song when they gather in a flock.
fields.hint: A bright red mask decorates my face.

fields.summary: A small, spotted brown bird with a thin, curved beak. It climbs up tree trunks in a spiral, looking for insects.
fields.size: 12.5 cm long, wingspan 17.5 to 20 cm, 8 to 12 g
fields.behaviour: It always climbs up the trunk in a spiral, probing the bark with its curved beak to find tiny insects and spiders. Then it flies down to the base of another tree.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods, parks and gardens with old trees that have rough bark. It tucks a hidden nest behind a loose piece of bark.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its wooded territory, without really migrating.
fields.by_ear: A short, high song, a little whistled and squeaky phrase. It is fairly quiet, and often the best clue for finding this well-camouflaged bird.
fields.confusions: It is very close to the Eurasian Treecreeper, which is rarer and lives in mountains in France. They are told apart mostly by song and by small feather details that are hard to see in the field.
fields.anecdote: Its spotted brown feathers blend so well with bark that you often spot it by its movement rather than its colour, like a tiny living piece of bark.
fields.hint: I always climb up the trunk, never down.

fields.summary: A small, very shy reddish-brown bird of wet thickets, known for its sudden, explosive song.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 15 to 19 cm, 12 to 18 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects in thick, damp plants. It stays almost invisible, creeping quietly through the bushes.
fields.why_here: It lives in wet thickets, bramble patches and stream edges with thick plants all year round.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year and does not migrate, despite its small size.
fields.by_ear: A sudden song, very strong and explosive for its size. It is a short, loud phrase thrown out without warning from a bush.
fields.confusions: You can hardly mix it up by song, which is very easy to know. By sight, it can look like other small brown birds, such as the Eurasian Wren.
fields.anecdote: Despite its tiny size, Cetti's Warbler sings so loudly and suddenly that it often startles people walking by.
fields.hint: My sudden, loud song bursts out of a hidden bush.

fields.summary: A stocky finch with olive-green feathers tinted with yellow, easiest to see on the wings and tail in flight.
fields.size: 14.5 to 16 cm long, wingspan 24.5 to 27.5 cm, 25 to 32 g
fields.behaviour: It eats mostly seeds, including big ones that it cracks with its strong beak. It often visits feeders, especially those with sunflower seeds.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks, hedges and edges, with trees to nest in and open ground to feed on. It often nests in small loose groups in conifers or thick hedges.
fields.migration: Some migrate in France. Some stay all year, others move locally or get visitors from northern Europe in winter.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk is one of its predators.
fields.by_ear: A song of varied trills with a typical nasal, drawn-out « dzwîî », a bit like an insistent complaint.
fields.confusions: From far away, it can be taken for a sparrow or a female Chaffinch. But the bright yellow on its wings in flight is a good clue.
fields.anecdote: Its nasal, drawn-out call, a bit like a yawn, is often one of the easiest sounds to know in gardens in spring once you have learned it.
fields.hint: Bright yellow flashes on my wings in flight.

fields.summary: A small gull with a chocolate-brown hood in summer. In winter, its head is white with a dark spot behind the eye.
fields.size: 34 to 37 cm long, wingspan 94 to 105 cm, 200 to 350 g
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything: insects, small fish and scraps. It likes to follow tractors to catch the worms they turn up.
fields.why_here: It lives at lakes, coasts, ploughed fields and in towns. It nests in colonies in wetlands with reedbeds.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. In winter, many more arrive from northern and eastern Europe.
fields.enemies: Crows and big gulls can eat its eggs or chicks. The Peregrine Falcon and the Northern Goshawk can also catch the adults.
fields.by_ear: A nasal, repeated « kiarr » or « kri-arr », called nonstop in the colonies.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with other small gulls. But its brown hood in summer, not black, and the dark spot behind the eye in winter tell it apart.
fields.anecdote: Despite its name, the hood of the Black-headed Gull in summer feathers is really chocolate brown, not black as people often think.
fields.hint: My summer hood is chocolate brown.

fields.summary: A big black and white wading bird with a red beak and red legs. In many regions, it is a sign that spring is back.
fields.size: 100 to 115 cm long, wingspan 195 to 215 cm, 2.3 to 4.4 kg
fields.behaviour: It eats frogs, insects, small rodents and worms in wet meadows. It nests in a big nest of sticks on poles or roofs.
fields.why_here: It lives in wet meadows, marshes and farmland where it finds plenty of food. It nests on high spots.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. Most fly back to Africa in August or September, but some groups now stay in France all year.
fields.by_ear: It is not very vocal. It mostly talks by loudly clapping its beak, with no real call.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Grey Heron in flight. But the stork flies with its neck stretched out, not folded, and has sharp black and white contrast.
fields.anecdote: The White Stork does not sing. It talks by clapping its beak in a rhythm, a behaviour called bill-clattering.
fields.hint: I don't sing. I clap my beak to talk.

fields.summary: A tiny streaky brown bird of wet meadows. You can know it by its bouncy flight and its call repeated in flight.
fields.size: 10 cm long, wingspan 12 to 14 cm, 6 to 9 g
fields.behaviour: It eats small insects in low grass. It sings in a typical bouncy flight, going up and down in rhythm.
fields.why_here: It lives in wet meadows, grassy wasteland and low reedbeds, mostly in southern France.
fields.migration: It stays all year in southern France. But hard winters can wipe out many of them.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, repeated « zip-zip-zip » called in rhythm with each bounce of the flight.
fields.confusions: It is hard to mix up thanks to its tiny size and its typical bouncy flight with a repeated call.
fields.anecdote: The Zitting Cisticola builds a nest shaped like a woven purse, made with spider webs and sewn between several grass stems.
fields.hint: Tiny, I call with every bounce of my flight.

fields.summary: The biggest European finch. You can know it by its huge, strong beak that can crack cherry stones.
fields.size: 16.5 to 18 cm long, wingspan 29 to 33 cm, 48 to 62 g
fields.behaviour: It eats hard seeds, stones and big pips, which it breaks with amazing beak strength. It often stays quiet, perched high in the trees.
fields.why_here: It lives in old broadleaf woods, parks and orchards with big trees such as hornbeams or wild cherries. It especially likes their stone fruits.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year. It makes only small local moves in winter, depending on food.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk and the Northern Goshawk can hunt it.
fields.by_ear: A short, sharp contact call, a typical metallic « tzik ». It is often the only sign it is there, because it stays quiet and perched high.
fields.confusions: Its heavy shape with a big head and a big beak sets it apart from all other finches in France, once you see it well.
fields.anecdote: Its beak squeezes so hard that it can crack cherry stones. That is a lot of strength for a bird this size.
fields.hint: My massive beak can crush a fruit stone.

fields.summary: A small grey and black crow with a very typical pale eye. It is sociable and lively.
fields.size: 33 to 34 cm long, wingspan 64 to 73 cm, 220 to 270 g
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything: insects, seeds and scraps. It nests in colonies in holes, bell towers, chimneys or old hollow trees.
fields.why_here: It likes villages, old buildings, cliffs and hedgerow farmland, which offer holes to nest in as a group.
fields.migration: Most stay in France all year. In winter, many northern birds arrive.
fields.enemies: The Northern Goshawk can hunt it.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, metallic call, a repeated « tchak » or « kya », often given in flight by whole groups.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Carrion Crow, which is much bigger and has no grey neck or pale eye.
fields.anecdote: The Western Jackdaw often picks its partner for life. Pairs stay together all year, even outside the breeding season.
fields.hint: My pale eye shines in my grey and black feathers.

fields.summary: The wild ancestor of the city pigeon. It is blue-grey with a white rump and two black bars on the wing, and city birds vary a lot.
fields.size: 31 to 34 cm long, wingspan 63 to 70 cm, 230 to 380 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and food scraps, often in big groups that are not afraid of people in towns. It nests on ledges or in buildings, like the cliffs of its wild ancestor.
fields.why_here: City Rock Doves come from escaped farm pigeons. They live in towns and villages, nesting on buildings as if they were artificial cliffs.
fields.migration: It stays all year in the same town or countryside area and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: The Peregrine Falcon often hunts it in flight.
fields.by_ear: A deep, repeated cooing, shorter and more rolling than the Common Wood Pigeon's. It is often heard nonstop near nesting sites.
fields.confusions: City pigeons have very varied feathers, from white to black to reddish. The Common Wood Pigeon is bigger, with a sharp white patch on the neck.
fields.anecdote: The original wild Rock Dove, which nests on rocky cliffs, still lives in a few remote places. Most city pigeons are its descendants that went wild again.
fields.hint: My wild ancestor nests on cliffs.

fields.summary: The biggest pigeon in Europe. It is blue-grey with a typical white patch on each side of the neck, and very common in towns and countryside.
fields.size: 40 to 42 cm long, wingspan 68 to 77 cm, 400 to 550 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds, buds, leaves and fruit, often in groups in fields. It takes off noisily, with a typical clap of its wings.
fields.why_here: It lives in forests, parks, gardens and big farm fields. It has adapted very well to towns in recent decades.
fields.migration: Some migrate. In autumn, some French wood pigeons fly to Spain in big flocks, while others stay all year, especially in towns.
fields.enemies: The Northern Goshawk can catch it in mid-air.
fields.by_ear: A deep, cooing song, a repeated five-syllable phrase that French people remember with a funny sentence. It is sung from a hidden perch.
fields.confusions: The Rock Dove is smaller with no white neck patch and has more varied feathers. The Eurasian Collared Dove is much smaller, with a thin black collar.
fields.anecdote: In autumn, tens of thousands of them can fly over some Pyrenees mountain passes in a single day.
fields.hint: A white patch decorates each side of my neck.

fields.summary: A big, all-black crow. It is more of a loner than the Rook, very adaptable and clever.
fields.size: 45 to 47 cm long, wingspan 93 to 104 cm, 370 to 650 g
fields.behaviour: It eats whatever it finds: insects, seeds, dead animals, eggs and scraps. It lives as a pair all year and defends a fixed territory for a long time.
fields.why_here: It fits almost anywhere, in countryside, towns and forests, as long as it finds food and trees to nest in.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A hoarse, deep croak, repeated three or four times, « craa-craa-craa ».
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Rook, which has a thinner beak with a pale base, and with the Western Jackdaw, which is smaller with a grey neck.
fields.anecdote: The Carrion Crow can make and use small tools to get food that is hard to reach.
fields.hint: All black, I live alone or in pairs, never in big flocks.

fields.summary: A big black crow with a thin beak. In adults, the base of the beak is greyish and bare. It is very sociable.
fields.size: 44 to 46 cm long, wingspan 81 to 94 cm, 400 to 500 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds mostly on the ground, on worms, grubs and seeds. It nests in big, noisy colonies at the very top of trees, often in the same place every year.
fields.why_here: It lives in open farmland, ploughed fields and meadows, where it easily finds food on the ground.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year. In winter, birds from northern and eastern Europe join it.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can catch the Rook.
fields.by_ear: A croak that is higher and more nasal than the Carrion Crow's, often heard from the noisy colonies.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Carrion Crow. But the Rook has a thinner beak, and in adults the base of the beak is pale and bare.
fields.anecdote: Rook colonies, called rookeries, can hold several hundred nests in the same trees, year after year.
fields.hint: I live in big noisy flocks at the tops of trees.

fields.summary: A slim grey bird that flies a bit like a bird of prey. It is famous for laying its eggs in other birds' nests, so they raise its chick for it.
fields.size: 32 to 34 cm long, wingspan 55 to 60 cm, 105 to 130 g
fields.behaviour: The female lays an egg in another bird's nest, often a small songbird's. That bird raises the chick without knowing it is not its own. It eats mostly hairy caterpillars.
fields.why_here: It lives in many open and wooded places in France, as long as host birds are around to raise its young, like the Dunnock or warblers.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in April and leaves as early as July or August, one of the first migrants to leave Europe. It spends winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.enemies: The calls of the chicks can attract foxes, weasels or birds of prey.
fields.by_ear: A very well-known song, a two-note « cuc-koo » repeated again and again in spring. That is how the bird got its name in many languages.
fields.confusions: In flight, its slim shape with pointed wings can look like a small bird of prey such as the Eurasian Sparrowhawk. That sometimes fools small birds and makes them give alarm calls.
fields.anecdote: Once hatched, the young cuckoo pushes the eggs or chicks of its host out of the nest. This way it gets all the food brought by its adoptive parents.
fields.hint: Other birds raise my chicks for me.

fields.summary: A warbler of open places. The male has a clear white throat and a grey head. It often perches on a bush or a wire.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 18 to 23 cm, 12 to 18 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects caught in low bushes and tall grass, and turns to berries in late summer. It is often seen singing in flight above hedges.
fields.why_here: It lives on wasteland, bushy hedges, field edges and banks with low, thorny plants to nest in.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in spring, in April, and leaves in late summer, in August or September, to spend winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.enemies: The house cat and the Red Fox are among its predators.
fields.by_ear: A fast, chatty song, a series of scratchy, cheerful notes. It is often sung in a little display flight above a hedge before the bird lands again.
fields.confusions: Its clear white throat and its song flights set it apart from the Garden Warbler, which is plainer and shyer.
fields.anecdote: The male often makes a little song flight above the bushes, rising and then dropping back, as if to get attention before landing.
fields.hint: I sing in a short display flight above a hedge.

fields.summary: A small, lively tit with a bright blue cap, white cheeks and a yellow-green back. It is very common in gardens all year.
fields.size: 11.5 cm long, wingspan 17.5 to 20 cm, 9 to 12 g
fields.behaviour: An agile acrobat, it checks the ends of thin branches and the undersides of leaves to find caterpillars and tiny insects. In winter, it loves sunflower seeds at feeders.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks and broadleaf woods, where it finds holes to nest in, natural ones or in a nest box. It especially likes oaks, full of caterpillars in spring.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with only small local moves. There is little big migration compared with other songbirds.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch it. The Great Spotted Woodpecker can take chicks from the nest.
fields.by_ear: A clear, fast song, a series of high notes followed by a fast, light trill. The usual call is a thin, piercing little « tsi-tsi-tsi ».
fields.confusions: Its blue cap and white cheeks easily set it apart from the Great Tit, which is bigger with a black head. At first glance it can be mixed up with the Marsh Tit, but that one has no blue.
fields.anecdote: A pair of Eurasian Blue Tits can feed their brood several hundred caterpillars a day when the chicks are growing fastest.
fields.hint: Pairs of us feed chicks hundreds of caterpillars a day.

fields.summary: A big, all-white water bird with an orange beak topped by a black bump, and an S-shaped neck.
fields.size: 125 to 160 cm long, wingspan 200 to 240 cm, 8 to 12 kg
fields.behaviour: It eats water plants by dipping its head and neck under the water. It can be very territorial and aggressive toward intruders.
fields.why_here: It lives at big lakes, ponds, calm rivers and city parks, where it finds plenty of water plants.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with a few local moves in winter.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox and crows can go after the young.
fields.by_ear: It is not very vocal. It gives soft grunts and hisses. The sound of its wings in flight is a typical whistling throb.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with Bewick's Swan or the Whooper Swan, which are rarer in France and have a yellow and black beak with no bump.
fields.anecdote: The rhythmic, whistling sound of its wings in flight lets you spot it even without seeing it.
fields.hint: A black bump sits at the base of my orange beak.

fields.summary: A small swallow with a shiny blue-black back and a white rump you can easily see in flight. It nests under roofs.
fields.size: 12.5 cm long, wingspan 26 to 29 cm, 15 to 21 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects in flight high in the sky. It builds a closed, cup-shaped mud nest stuck under the edges of roofs.
fields.why_here: It lives in towns and villages, where it finds sheltered spots to build its mud nest under the eaves.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa in September or October.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Hobby can hunt it in flight.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, creaky « prrit » call, and a quiet, twittering song that is weaker than the Barn Swallow's.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Barn Swallow, which has a red throat and a more forked tail, and with the Common Swift, which is all black and sickle-shaped.
fields.anecdote: The Western House Martin builds its nest with balls of mud carried one by one, sometimes several thousand for a single nest.
fields.hint: My white rump flashes below my blue-black back in flight.

fields.summary: The most common woodpecker in France. It has sharp black and white feathers with a red patch under the tail. The male also has a red patch on the back of the neck.
fields.size: 22 to 23 cm long, wingspan 34 to 39 cm, 70 to 98 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for insects under bark and in dead wood by hammering trunks with its strong beak. It also eats seeds and hazelnuts, which it wedges in a crack in the bark to open them.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods, parks and gardens with big trees, especially ones with dead wood where it can dig its nest hole.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its territory. Sometimes birds from the north arrive in large numbers in years when seeds are scarce.
fields.enemies: The Northern Goshawk and the Eurasian Sparrowhawk can hunt it.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, loud call, a clear single « kick ». In spring, it drums fast on a ringing branch to mark its territory, rather than singing.
fields.confusions: The Lesser Spotted Woodpecker, much smaller, has no red under the tail. The Middle Spotted Woodpecker, rarer, has a fully red cap in both sexes.
fields.anecdote: Its drumming, made by hitting a branch up to about twenty times a second, works as a territory signal instead of a sung song.
fields.hint: I drum on wood instead of singing.

fields.summary: The smallest woodpecker in Europe, barely bigger than a sparrow. Its feathers are barred black and white, with no red patch under the tail.
fields.size: 14 to 16.5 cm long, wingspan 25 to 27 cm, 18 to 26 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for small insects on thin branches and in dead wood high up. It is often quiet and hard to spot in the treetops.
fields.why_here: It lives in broadleaf woods, old orchards and big gardens with old trees or dead wood high up.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its territory and hardly moves.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can hunt it. The Great Spotted Woodpecker can also take its chicks.
fields.by_ear: A high, repeated call, a series of thin notes. Its drumming is longer and softer than the Great Spotted Woodpecker's.
fields.confusions: It is much smaller than the Great Spotted Woodpecker and has no red under the tail. Still, because of its small size, it can go unnoticed in the treetops.
fields.anecdote: It spends most of its time at the very top of trees. That makes it much harder to see than other woodpeckers, even though it is fairly widespread.
fields.hint: I live at the very top of trees, hard to spot.

fields.summary: The biggest woodpecker in Europe. It is all black with a red cap. Male and female differ by how much red they have on the head.
fields.size: 45 to 57 cm long, wingspan 64 to 68 cm, 250 to 370 g
fields.behaviour: It digs big, rectangular holes in trunks to find carpenter ants and beetle grubs deep in the wood. Its flight is strong and direct.
fields.why_here: It lives in big old forests, of broadleaf trees or conifers, with old trees big enough for its large nest hole.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, on a large forest territory, and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Pine Marten can eat the eggs and chicks in the nest hole.
fields.by_ear: A strong, clear call, a long sad cry that carries far through the forest. It also drums very loudly, for a long time and at an even rhythm, which can be heard from far away.
fields.confusions: Its huge size and all-black feathers mean you cannot mix it up with other woodpeckers in France, which are all much smaller.
fields.anecdote: The big holes it leaves behind are reused by many other species, such as some owls or bats. That makes it a key species for the forest.
fields.hint: My big nest hole is later used by other animals.

fields.summary: A small, elegant, all-white heron with a thin black beak and black legs ending in yellow feet.
fields.size: 55 to 65 cm long, wingspan 88 to 106 cm, 350 to 550 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts actively, walking quickly in shallow water. Sometimes it wiggles a yellow foot to flush out its prey.
fields.why_here: It lives on mudflats, shallow ponds, marshes and seashores, where it finds fish and small animals without backbones.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year, mostly in the south. Some fly farther south in winter.
fields.enemies: Birds of prey and crows can attack the chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A hoarse, creaky call that is not very musical. It is given mostly around the nesting colonies.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Cattle Egret, which has a yellow beak and is stockier, or with a young Great Egret, which is bigger.
fields.anecdote: The Little Egret nearly disappeared from Europe in the 19th century. It was hunted for its fancy feathers used in hats.
fields.hint: All white, my yellow feet stand out against my black legs.

fields.summary: A big, stocky, dull bunting, streaky brown with little colour contrast. It is typical of big grain-growing plains.
fields.size: 18 cm long, wingspan 26 to 32 cm, 38 to 55 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects on the ground. It sings from an electric wire or a stem in full view.
fields.why_here: It lives in big open farm plains, grain fields and rough meadows with few trees.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with a few local moves linked to winter food.
fields.enemies: The Barn Owl and Montagu's Harrier can catch the Corn Bunting.
fields.by_ear: A dry, metallic song, compared to the sound of a bunch of keys being shaken, without much music in it.
fields.confusions: It is hard to mix up thanks to its bigger size and its dull look with no clear marks.
fields.anecdote: The Corn Bunting often flies with its legs dangling, a clumsy pose that is typical of the species on short flights.
fields.hint: My song sounds like a bunch of keys being shaken.

fields.summary: A small bunting close to the Yellowhammer. The male has a black throat and a yellow stripe over the eye. It lives more in the south.
fields.size: 15.5 cm long, wingspan 22 to 25.5 cm, 20 to 27 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects on the ground. It sings from a perch in sunny hedges or bushes.
fields.why_here: It lives on sunny slopes, vineyards, orchards and bushy hedges, mostly in the south and west of France.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with few seasonal moves.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can attack the adults. Eggs and chicks may also be taken by the Red-backed Shrike or the Eurasian Jay.
fields.by_ear: A dry, flat song, a sort of fast trill on a single note. It is shorter and less musical than the Yellowhammer's.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Yellowhammer, but the male Cirl Bunting has a black throat and mask and less yellow on the head.
fields.anecdote: The Cirl Bunting is much more local in France than the Yellowhammer. It prefers regions with a mild, sunny climate.
fields.hint: My black throat sets me apart from my yellower cousin.

fields.summary: A small countryside bird. The male is bright yellow. It is typical of hedges and hedgerow farmland.
fields.size: 16 to 17 cm long, wingspan 23 to 29 cm, 24 to 30 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects on the ground. It often sings in full view at the top of a hedge or a bush.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedgerow farmland, country hedges and crop edges, where it finds seeds and low nesting spots in the plants.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with a few local moves in winter depending on food.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. Crows and magpies can also eat the eggs or chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A rhythmic song, often put into words as « a little bit of bread and no cheese », ending with a drawn-out note.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Cirl Bunting, but the male Yellowhammer is much yellower on the head and chest.
fields.anecdote: The Yellowhammer's song is one of the easiest to remember, thanks to a well-known phrase that helps people learn it.
fields.hint: My song sounds like a sentence about bread and cheese.

fields.summary: A small bunting of wet places. In breeding feathers, the male has a black head and a sharp white collar.
fields.size: 15.5 cm long, wingspan 21 to 28 cm, 15 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects, often on the ground near water or clinging to reed stems.
fields.why_here: It lives in reedbeds, marshes and pond edges with thick plants, where it finds food and shelter to nest.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Birds from the north come to spend the winter here, from October to March.
fields.enemies: The Western Marsh Harrier can catch the Common Reed Bunting.
fields.by_ear: A simple, repeated song, a few creaky notes sung from the top of a reed.
fields.confusions: The male in breeding feathers, with a black head and a white collar, is hard to mix up. The streaky brown female can look like a sparrow.
fields.anecdote: The Common Reed Bunting often perches in plain view at the top of the reeds to sing, unlike other, shyer marsh birds.
fields.hint: My black head and white collar stand out above the stems.

fields.summary: A small, round bird with a bright orange breast. It is very common in gardens and not very shy of people.
fields.size: 12 to 14 cm long, wingspan 20 to 22 cm, 16 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects, worms and small fruit on the ground, often alone outside the breeding season. It firmly defends its territory all year, even in winter, standing straight up on a low perch.
fields.why_here: It likes gardens, hedges, undergrowth and edges with loose soil to hunt in. It nests low, in a thick bush, an ivy-covered wall or an odd hiding place like a flowerpot.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year. In winter, robins from northern and eastern Europe join it, escaping the cold. So you can see it in our gardens all year.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Pine Marten, jays and crows can take the eggs or chicks of the European Robin from the nest.
fields.by_ear: A smooth, crystal-clear song, a string of high, pearly notes that seem to hesitate and then speed up. It is often heard early in the morning, or even at night near street lamps. Its alarm call is a sharp, repeated « tic ».
fields.confusions: The young bird is spotted brown with no orange patch, which can be confusing before autumn. From far away it can be mixed up with a Dunnock, which never has orange on its chest.
fields.anecdote: It sometimes sings at night under a street lamp, as if it thought the artificial light was the sunrise.
fields.hint: My breast is the colour of an autumn fruit.

fields.summary: A small, slim bird of prey with pointed wings. It is famous for hovering in the wind, staying still in the air to spot its prey.
fields.size: 32 to 35 cm long, wingspan 65 to 82 cm, 136 to 314 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts mostly small rodents, which it spots from its typical hover. It beats its wings fast to stay still facing the wind, then dives on its prey.
fields.why_here: It lives in open countryside as well as in towns. It nests on building ledges, cliffs or old crow nests, and hunts over fields, meadows or wasteland.
fields.migration: Some migrate in France. Some stay all year, while others fly south in winter, sometimes replaced by falcons from the north.
fields.enemies: The Northern Goshawk can catch the adults.
fields.by_ear: A high, repeated call, a series of piercing « ki-ki-ki ». It is mostly heard near the nest or in display flights, and quieter outside the breeding season.
fields.confusions: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk has shorter, rounded wings and never hovers. The Common Kestrel has pointed wings and that special hovering flight.
fields.anecdote: Its hovering into the wind lets it spot even vole urine trails, which glow in ultraviolet light that human eyes cannot see.
fields.hint: I stay still in mid-air, facing the wind.

fields.summary: A very common, colourful songbird. The male has a pinkish breast and a blue-grey head. The female is duller and olive-brown.
fields.size: 14.5 cm long, wingspan 24.5 to 28.5 cm, 18 to 29 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds on the ground and in trees on seeds, buds and insects, depending on the season. Outside the breeding season, it often joins mixed groups, especially with other finches.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks, woods and hedges, almost anywhere with trees. It builds a very neat cup nest, decorated with lichen, in a fork of a branch.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Some French chaffinches stay all year, while others come from northern Europe to spend the winter here, often in big flocks.
fields.enemies: Crows, squirrels and cats can take the eggs and chicks of the Eurasian Chaffinch.
fields.by_ear: A lively, falling song, a cascade of notes that speeds up and ends with a clear final flourish. It is often described as a phrase that « rolls down the slope ».
fields.confusions: The olive-brown female can be mixed up with a sparrow. But she has two sharp white bars on the wing, which sparrows do not have.
fields.anecdote: Its Latin name « coelebs » means « bachelor ». People had noticed that in winter in northern Europe, males and females often split into separate groups.
fields.hint: Two white bars cross my wing.

fields.summary: An all-black water bird with a clear white beak and a white patch on the forehead. It is stockier than the Moorhen.
fields.size: 36 to 38 cm long, wingspan 70 to 80 cm, 600 to 900 g
fields.behaviour: It dives to eat water plants. It can be very aggressive toward others of its kind, especially in the breeding season.
fields.why_here: It lives at big ponds, lakes and calm rivers with water plants, where it finds plenty of food.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year. In winter, birds from northern Europe join it.
fields.enemies: The American Mink and the Red Fox can take the chicks of the Eurasian Coot. Harriers and crows also attack the broods.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, loud, metallic « kroik » or « kvek », called often, especially in groups.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Common Moorhen, which is smaller and has a red beak, not a white one.
fields.anecdote: The Eurasian Coot can be very aggressive. It chases and attacks others of its kind to defend its territory.
fields.hint: My white beak and forehead patch stand out against my black feathers.

fields.summary: A small, stocky lark with dull beige-brown feathers. You can know it by the pointed crest standing up on its head.
fields.size: 17 cm long, wingspan 29 to 38 cm, 35 to 45 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects on the ground. It walks more than it flies and often stays near bare ground.
fields.why_here: It lives on wasteland, rough ground, roadsides and in towns or industrial areas with bare ground and few plants.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: Crows and magpies can attack its nests.
fields.by_ear: A sad, flute-like « dliu-dliu » call. Its simple song is given on the ground or in low flight.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Eurasian Skylark. But the Crested Lark is stockier, has a visible crest and does not sing in long, steep flights.
fields.anecdote: The Crested Lark has become very rare in France, as the wasteland and rough ground it loves have disappeared.
fields.hint: I walk more than I fly, and stay near bare ground.

fields.summary: A black water bird with a red beak tipped in yellow and a red patch on the forehead. Its tail is held up and shows white.
fields.size: 32 to 35 cm long, wingspan 50 to 55 cm, 250 to 400 g
fields.behaviour: It swims with a nodding head. It eats water plants and small animals without backbones at the edges of ponds.
fields.why_here: It lives at ponds, pools and rivers with thick plants along the edge, where it finds food and shelter to nest.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, with a few local moves in winter if the water freezes.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox and the American Mink can catch its chicks. The Western Marsh Harrier can also hunt them.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, loud call, a sort of « krrrk » or a short cluck, often given at night.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Eurasian Coot, which is bigger, all black with a white beak and forehead patch.
fields.anecdote: Despite its name, the Common Moorhen is not a chicken. It belongs to the rail family and is related to coots.
fields.hint: My red beak with a yellow tip stands out against black.

fields.summary: A crow-family bird with pinkish-brown feathers and a blue wing patch barred with black. It is shy despite its bright colours.
fields.size: 34 to 35 cm long, wingspan 52 to 58 cm, 140 to 190 g
fields.behaviour: It eats mostly acorns, which it hides in autumn for winter. That helps spread oak trees. It also eats insects, fruit and sometimes eggs or chicks.
fields.why_here: It lives in broadleaf forests and wooded parks with lots of oaks, where it finds plenty of acorns and holes to nest in.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year and does not migrate, though some northern birds may move locally in winter.
fields.enemies: Martens can eat the eggs and chicks in the nest. Birds of prey can catch the adults and the young that have just left the nest.
fields.by_ear: A hoarse, creaky call, often compared to ripping cloth. It also copies the call of the Common Buzzard very well.
fields.confusions: It is hard to mix up thanks to its blue wing patch and white rump, which are easy to see in flight.
fields.anecdote: A single Eurasian Jay can hide several thousand acorns in autumn and forget a good part of them. That helps new oak forests grow.
fields.hint: I hide acorns everywhere, but I forget many of them.

fields.summary: A small, shy green-yellow bird, famous for its chatty song that mixes copies and varied phrases nonstop.
fields.size: 13 cm long, wingspan 18 to 21 cm, 9 to 13 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects in thick leaves. It sings very fast from a perch that is often hidden in the plants.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedges, thick bushes, gardens and woodland edges with bushy plants to hide and nest in.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.by_ear: A fast, chatty, varied song, linking phrases without a pause, sometimes copying other birds. It is a real nonstop stream.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Eurasian Blackcap or other small greenish birds. But its fast, nonstop song is very special.
fields.anecdote: Its name « polyglotta » comes from its song, which seems to mix all kinds of sounds and copies without ever stopping.
fields.hint: My chatty song strings phrases together without stopping.

fields.summary: A swallow with a long forked tail and a red throat. It is a sign of spring, coming back to the same farms every year.
fields.size: 17 to 19 cm long with the long tail streamers, wingspan 32 to 34.5 cm, 16 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects in fast, low flight, often over meadows and streams. It builds a mud nest inside buildings.
fields.why_here: It lives on farms, in barns and cowsheds, where it finds beams to nest on and plenty of insects near the animals.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in March or April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in September or October.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch young birds that have just left the nest.
fields.by_ear: A continuous, twittering song, a mix of trills and happy chirps, often sung in flight or perched on a wire.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Western House Martin, which has a blue back and a white rump, and with the Common Swift, which has sickle-shaped wings and a shrill scream.
fields.anecdote: A Barn Swallow can travel thousands of kilometres every year to reach the same farms, first in Africa and then in Europe.
fields.hint: My throat is red and my tail ends in two long streamers.

fields.summary: A small bird with a hooked beak. The male has a grey head and a black mask. It is known for spearing its prey on thorns.
fields.size: 17 cm long, wingspan 24 to 27 cm, 25 to 35 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts big insects, small lizards and sometimes chicks. It spears its prey on thorns or barbed wire to keep it as a food store.
fields.why_here: It lives in thorny hedges, hedgerow farmland and bushy wasteland, where it finds thorns to store its prey.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in May and flies to southern Africa as early as August or September.
fields.enemies: Magpies and crows can eat its eggs or chicks.
fields.by_ear: A song that is not very musical, mixing copies of other birds with creaky, varied notes.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with other shrikes that are rarer in France. But the male's black mask and reddish-brown back are fairly clear.
fields.anecdote: Its nickname « butcher bird » comes from its habit of spearing prey on thorns to store it or tear it apart.
fields.hint: I spear my prey on thorns to keep it for later.

fields.summary: A big gull with a light grey back and pink legs, and a yellow beak with a red spot. It is typical of northern coasts.
fields.size: 55 to 67 cm long, wingspan 130 to 158 cm, 800 g to 1.5 kg
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything it finds: fish, scraps, eggs and small animals. It visits harbours and rubbish tips looking for food.
fields.why_here: It lives on rocky and sandy coasts, in river mouths and in harbours, especially on the English Channel and North Atlantic coasts.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Numbers grow in winter when birds from the north arrive.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox can eat its eggs or chicks.
fields.by_ear: A strong, hoarse call, a series of loud « kaow », very like the Yellow-legged Gull's.
fields.confusions: It is often mixed up with the Yellow-legged Gull, but the European Herring Gull's pink legs, not yellow, tell them apart.
fields.anecdote: The European Herring Gull can drop shellfish on rocks or tarmac to break them and reach the soft flesh.
fields.hint: My pink legs set me apart from my cousin with yellow legs.

fields.summary: A big gull with a light grey back, yellow legs and a yellow beak with a red spot. It is very common on the coast and in towns.
fields.size: 52 to 58 cm long, wingspan 120 to 140 cm, 750 g to 1.2 kg
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything it finds: fish, scraps, eggs and small animals. It has adapted well to coastal towns and rubbish tips.
fields.why_here: It lives on coasts, in harbours, coastal towns and along big rivers, where it finds plenty of food and roofs to nest on.
fields.migration: Most stay in France all year, especially on the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox can eat its eggs or chicks.
fields.by_ear: A strong, hoarse call, a series of loud, repeated « kaow », typical of gulls.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the European Herring Gull, but the Yellow-legged Gull's yellow legs, not pink, tell them apart.
fields.anecdote: The Yellow-legged Gull has settled well in coastal towns, sometimes nesting right on the roofs of buildings.
fields.hint: I nest on roofs in coastal towns.

fields.summary: A small brown finch. In spring, the male has a pinkish forehead and breast. It is known for its varied, pleasant song.
fields.size: 13.5 cm long, wingspan 21 to 25.5 cm, 15 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It eats mostly small seeds of wild plants, on the ground and in low plants. It is sociable and forms groups outside the breeding season.
fields.why_here: It lives on wasteland, moors, bushy hedges and field edges with seed-rich plants. It nests low in a thorny bush such as gorse or hawthorn.
fields.migration: Some migrate in France. Some stay, while others fly south for winter. Meanwhile linnets from northern Europe may spend the winter here.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk sometimes catches the Common Linnet.
fields.by_ear: A varied, twittering song, mixing trills and musical notes strung together with no fixed pattern. It is often sung from a bush or in flight.
fields.confusions: The brown female with no pink can look like a Eurasian Tree Sparrow. But she has a thinner beak and no black spot on the cheek.
fields.anecdote: Its name recalls its taste for wild hemp and flax seeds, which were part of its traditional diet in the countryside.
fields.hint: My forehead turns pink in spring.

fields.summary: A tit that is easy to know by its pointed black and white crest. It lives only in conifer forests.
fields.size: 11.5 cm long, wingspan 17 to 20 cm, 9 to 13 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for food in conifer needles and bark, eating insects and conifer seeds. Like the Coal Tit, it hides seeds for the winter.
fields.why_here: It lives almost only in old pine and spruce forests, where it finds both food and old trunks to dig its nest hole in.
fields.migration: It stays all year in its conifer forest and hardly moves.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk and the Tawny Owl can catch the adults. Martens can also attack the chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A special song, a rather deep, purring, vibrating roll, different from the whistles of other tits. Its typical call is a little rolling trill that is easy to know once you have learned it.
fields.confusions: Its pointed crest makes it unique among European tits. You cannot mix it up if you see it well.
fields.anecdote: It lives only in old conifer forests and quickly disappears when they are cut down. That makes it a good sign of old forests.
fields.hint: I live only in old conifer forests.

fields.summary: A small, shy, dull brown bird, but famous for its powerful, varied song, often heard at night.
fields.size: 16 cm long, wingspan 23 to 26 cm, 18 to 27 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects and worms on the ground in thick plants. It stays very hidden despite its strong song.
fields.why_here: It lives in thick bushes, bramble patches and damp undergrowth with low, bushy plants to hide in.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.enemies: The Tawny Owl can catch the Common Nightingale.
fields.by_ear: A powerful, varied, flute-like song with rising trills and a famous repeated crescendo, sung at night as well as by day.
fields.confusions: You can hardly mix it up by song. By sight, it can look like a Dunnock or a female redstart because of its dull brown feathers.
fields.anecdote: The Common Nightingale sings at night as well as by day, unlike most songbirds. That has led to many legends.
fields.hint: My song is loud and varied, with a famous rising crescendo.

fields.summary: A brightly coloured bird with a golden-brown back, a blue-green belly and a yellow throat. It is an agile hunter of flying insects.
fields.size: 27 to 29 cm long with the long tail streamers, wingspan 36 to 40 cm, 44 to 78 g
fields.behaviour: It catches bees, wasps and other insects in acrobatic flight. Then it rubs them on a perch to remove the sting before swallowing them.
fields.why_here: It lives on sandy slopes, in quarries and on soft banks, where it digs a burrow to nest, often in colonies.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and flies to Africa from late summer, in August or September.
fields.enemies: Snakes can reach the chicks in their burrow.
fields.by_ear: A musical, rolling « prrruit » called in flight, often in groups. It is easy to spot even from far away.
fields.confusions: Few birds in Europe can be mixed up with it, thanks to its many bright colours, which are unique among birds in our regions.
fields.anecdote: The European Bee-eater can eat a bee after removing its sting, and it never gets stung.
fields.hint: Multicoloured, I rub my prey on a perch to remove its sting.

fields.summary: A big brown bird of prey with a slightly notched tail, often seen gliding in groups near rivers or rubbish tips.
fields.size: 48 to 58 cm long, wingspan 130 to 155 cm, 630 to 940 g
fields.behaviour: It eats dead fish, dead animals and small animals, often in groups around food sources like rubbish tips or riverbanks. Its gliding is very skilful, with frequent twists of the tail to change direction.
fields.why_here: It lives by rivers, lakes and open countryside with tall trees to nest in, often in small loose colonies.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in March and leaves as early as August or September to spend winter in Africa south of the Sahara. It is one of the most gregarious birds of prey on migration.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A rather high, whinnying call, a series of trembling, whistled notes, often given in flight. It is different from the mew of the Common Buzzard.
fields.confusions: Its tail, notched in the middle and easy to see in flight, sets it apart from the Common Buzzard, which has a rounded tail, and from the bigger, redder kites found elsewhere in Europe.
fields.anecdote: It can grab fish or floating scraps right from the water surface without landing, in a very precise skimming flight.
fields.hint: My tail has a slight notch in the middle.

fields.summary: A big bird of prey with a long, forked, reddish tail. You can know it in flight by its bent, angular wings.
fields.size: 60 to 66 cm long, wingspan 175 to 195 cm, 800 to 1300 g
fields.behaviour: It is an opportunistic scavenger. It also eats small mammals, earthworms and insects. It often visits open rubbish tips and nests in tall trees, often with the same mate year after year.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedgerow farmland with woods and meadows, where it easily spots dead animals and small prey while gliding over fields.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Many Red Kites nesting in France stay all year, while others from northern Europe spend the winter here, from October to March.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl can attack the adults and nests of the Red Kite.
fields.by_ear: A sad, flute-like call, a sort of high, repeated mew « hiiii-ha-ha-ha », quite different from the lower whistle of the Black Kite.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Black Kite, which has a less forked tail and darker feathers, and with the Common Buzzard, which has a rounded tail and no reddish colour.
fields.anecdote: The Red Kite nearly disappeared from France in the 20th century. It sometimes slips odd things like plastic or rags into its nest.
fields.hint: I almost vanished from France in the last century.

fields.summary: A small grey, white and black bird with a long tail that it keeps bobbing up and down.
fields.size: 18 cm long, wingspan 25 to 30 cm, 17 to 27 g
fields.behaviour: It walks on the ground, bobbing its tail, to catch insects. It often lives in open areas near water or homes.
fields.why_here: It likes yards, car parks, riverbanks and meadows, where it easily finds insects to hunt on the ground.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Some fly south in winter, while others stay.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk sometimes catches the White Wagtail.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, two-syllable « tchi-zik » called in flight, and a quiet, twittering song.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Grey Wagtail, which has a yellow belly and a longer tail, rather than with the Western Yellow Wagtail, which is green on top.
fields.anecdote: In winter, hundreds of White Wagtails can gather to sleep together on roofs or in city trees.
fields.hint: I walk on the ground near water and homes, hunting insects.

fields.summary: A slim bird with a bright yellow belly and a grey back, always near fast water. Its tail is very long.
fields.size: 18 to 19 cm long with a very long tail, wingspan 25 to 27 cm, 15 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts water insects by hopping on rocks and pebbles, bobbing its long tail all the time.
fields.why_here: It lives by fast, rocky streams, mountain brooks and rivers with a quick current, where it finds its prey.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Some move down to the lowlands or to the south in winter.
fields.enemies: The Peregrine Falcon and the Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A sharp « tsit-sit » call, higher than the White Wagtail's, and a creaky, weak song.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Western Yellow Wagtail. But the Grey Wagtail has a grey back, not green, and a much longer tail.
fields.anecdote: Despite its name, the Grey Wagtail sometimes nests quite far from water, in holes in walls or bridges.
fields.hint: I hop on rocks in fast streams, hunting water insects.

fields.summary: A small wagtail with an olive-green back and a bright yellow underside. It is typical of wet meadows in spring.
fields.size: 17 cm long, wingspan 23 to 27 cm, 15 to 20 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects on the ground in meadows, often among farm animals, catching the flies they stir up as they pass.
fields.why_here: It lives in wet meadows, crops and pastures with farm animals, where it finds plenty of insects within reach.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara as early as August or September.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox and crows can eat its eggs or chicks in the nest on the ground.
fields.by_ear: A short « tsip » or « psiit » call given in flight, and a simple, plain song.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Grey Wagtail. But the Western Yellow Wagtail has a green back, not grey, and a shorter tail.
fields.anecdote: The Western Yellow Wagtail happily follows herds of cows or sheep to eat the insects they stir up while grazing.
fields.hint: I follow cows and sheep to snap up flies.

fields.summary: A small, shy, streaky grey-brown bird. You can know it by its upright posture and its short flights to catch insects.
fields.size: 14.5 cm long, wingspan 23 to 25.5 cm, 14 to 20 g
fields.behaviour: It watches for flying insects from a fixed perch, flies out briefly to catch them, then often comes back to the same spot.
fields.why_here: It lives in parks, orchards, gardens and woodland edges with open perches for hunting flying insects.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in May and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara as early as August or September. It is one of the last to arrive in spring.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Jay can eat the eggs or chicks in the nest. Cats can also catch the young.
fields.by_ear: A quiet, plain song, a few creaky notes with no real tune. It often goes unnoticed.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with other small brown birds, but its upright posture and its short flights out and back from a perch are special.
fields.anecdote: The Spotted Flycatcher often comes back to exactly the same perch after each hunting trip, like a guard faithful to his post.
fields.hint: I wait, still, then dash out and return to the same spot.

fields.summary: A bird with bright yellow and black feathers in the male. It is very colourful but shy, because it stays hidden in the leaves.
fields.size: 22 to 25 cm long, wingspan 44 to 47 cm, 50 to 90 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects and fruit in the treetops. It stays high up in the trees and is rarely seen, despite its bright colours.
fields.why_here: It lives in big broadleaf trees, poplar groves, orchards and light woods, where it hides in the thick leaves.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and flies to Africa south of the Sahara as early as late summer, in August.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Magpie and the Carrion Crow can raid the nest of the Eurasian Golden Oriole.
fields.by_ear: A flute-like, melodious song, often put into words as « pirou-pirou-lio ». It is easy to spot even when the bird stays out of sight.
fields.confusions: The yellow and black male is hard to mix up with other species. The greener female can look like a big green songbird.
fields.anecdote: Despite its bright colours, the Eurasian Golden Oriole stays so well hidden in the leaves that you hear it much more often than you see it.
fields.hint: Very colourful yet hidden, I am heard more than seen.

fields.summary: A tiny grey or brown owl with small feather tufts. It is a migrant of the Mediterranean, heard more often than seen.
fields.size: 19 to 20 cm long, wingspan 47 to 54 cm, 60 to 135 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts mostly big insects like grasshoppers and moths, caught in flight or on the ground in the dark. By day, it stays very quiet and still, pressed against a trunk.
fields.why_here: It lives in old villages, orchards and light groves in the south of France, where it finds holes to nest in and plenty of insects on warm summer nights.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in April and leaves as early as September to spend winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.enemies: The Tawny Owl can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A very easy-to-know song, a short, whistled « pyoo » repeated at regular spaces all night. It is often the only sign it is there, because it stays so well hidden.
fields.confusions: It is much smaller than the Little Owl or the Tawny Owl. Its whistled, steady song, repeated all night with no change, makes it easy to know.
fields.anecdote: Its camouflage is so perfect, pressed against tree bark during the day, that it is almost impossible to spot by sight, even when you know where to look.
fields.hint: My song whistles the same note all night.

fields.summary: The biggest tit in Europe. You can know it by its black and white head and the black tie on its yellow chest.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 22 to 25 cm, 16 to 21 g
fields.behaviour: Very busy, it explores branches and bark looking for insects, caterpillars and seeds. It often visits feeders in winter, where it can boss around other tits.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks, woods and hedges, anywhere it finds a hole to nest in, natural or a nest box put up by people.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its territory, sometimes joined in winter by a few birds from northern Europe.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. The Great Spotted Woodpecker can also attack the chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A much-repeated song, a loud « ti-ta, ti-ta, ti-ta » like the sound of a saw being sharpened, sung nonstop in spring. Many other calls all year.
fields.confusions: Its black tie, wider and running down to the belly in the male, sets it apart from the Eurasian Blue Tit, which is smaller and has no black on the chest.
fields.anecdote: Some Great Tits learned to open milk bottles left on doorsteps to drink the cream. This was seen in the last century in the United Kingdom.
fields.hint: A black tie runs across my yellow chest.

fields.summary: A small brown and grey bird that is very used to people. The male has a black bib and a grey cap. The female is duller.
fields.size: 14 to 16 cm long, wingspan 21 to 25.5 cm, 24 to 39.5 g
fields.behaviour: It always lives near people, eating seeds, crumbs and insects, often in noisy flocks. It takes dust baths to keep its feathers in shape.
fields.why_here: It is closely tied to homes. It nests in holes in roofs, garden hedges or nest boxes, using the food that people provide.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year near the same buildings and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk sometimes catches the adult House Sparrow.
fields.by_ear: A simple, repeated call, a string of rather loud « chip-chip », given in a group from a hedge or a roof. It has no real musical song.
fields.confusions: The Eurasian Tree Sparrow, which is rarer, has a brown cap and a black spot on its white cheek. The male House Sparrow has a grey cap and no spot on the cheek.
fields.anecdote: It used to be extremely common. It has dropped sharply in many European cities, and the causes are still debated.
fields.hint: Once extremely common, I have become much rarer in many cities.

fields.summary: A more countryside cousin of the House Sparrow. It has a brown cap and a black spot on its white cheek. Male and female look the same.
fields.size: 12.5 to 14 cm long, wingspan 20 to 22 cm, 19 to 25 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds and insects, often in groups in fields and orchards. It is shyer and less tied to people than the House Sparrow.
fields.why_here: It lives in countryside, orchards, hedgerows and villages, more in rural areas than in big cities. It nests in a hole, in an old wall, a hollow tree or a nest box.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, sometimes moving locally in winter to gather around food sources.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk catches the Eurasian Tree Sparrow.
fields.by_ear: A call fairly close to the House Sparrow's but a bit higher, a sharp « tek-tek », often given in flight by small groups.
fields.confusions: It differs from the House Sparrow by its brown cap covering the whole head and its round black spot on the white cheek, found in both sexes.
fields.anecdote: Unlike the House Sparrow, male and female Tree Sparrows look almost the same, which is fairly rare among songbirds.
fields.hint: A round black spot marks my pale cheek.

fields.summary: A small, shy tit with a black and white head and a white patch on the back of the neck. It lives with conifers.
fields.size: 11.5 cm long, wingspan 17 to 21 cm, 7 to 11 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for food mostly in conifers, pecking conifer seeds and tiny insects hidden in the needles. It often hides seeds for winter, one by one, in the bark.
fields.why_here: It lives mostly in conifer forests, but also visits gardens with firs or pines, especially in winter when it comes down to the lowlands.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year. Sometimes birds from the north or east arrive in winter when conifer seeds are scarce there.
fields.by_ear: A simple, repeated song, a clear « ti-tu, ti-tu, ti-tu », thinner and faster than the Great Tit's.
fields.confusions: Its clear white patch on the back of the neck sets it apart from other black-headed tits. It is smaller and slimmer than the Great Tit, with no yellow on the body.
fields.anecdote: It can hide thousands of conifer seeds in autumn, scattered all over, and then finds most of them again thanks to its memory.
fields.hint: A small white patch decorates the back of my head.

fields.summary: A big black bird with a hooked beak. It often stands with its wings spread out to dry after diving.
fields.size: 80 to 100 cm long, wingspan 130 to 160 cm, 2 to 2.5 kg
fields.behaviour: It dives and swims underwater to catch fish. Its feathers are not very waterproof, so it dries them by spreading its wings in the sun.
fields.why_here: It lives at big lakes, rivers and coasts full of fish. It nests in colonies in trees or on cliffs.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. In winter, birds from northern Europe join them.
fields.enemies: At the nest, gulls and crows can take its eggs or chicks if the colony is disturbed.
