fields.by_ear: It is not very vocal outside the colonies. It makes hoarse, throaty grunts near the nest.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the European Shag, which is rarer in France and lives only at sea, or from far away in flight with a black goose.
fields.anecdote: Unlike most water birds, the cormorant's feathers are not fully waterproof, so it has to dry them often.
fields.hint: After diving, I spread my black wings to dry.

fields.summary: A big bird the size of a chicken. The male is very colourful with a long tail. The brown female is harder to notice.
fields.size: male 70 to 90 cm with the long tail, female 55 to 65 cm, wingspan 70 to 90 cm, 900 g to 1.6 kg
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds, insects and small animals without backbones on the ground. When disturbed, it takes off noisily for a short flight.
fields.why_here: It lives in light woods, edges, crops and hedges. It is often released for hunting, and it is now well settled in our countryside.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox can hunt the adult Common Pheasant and attack its eggs.
fields.by_ear: The male gives a loud, hoarse call, a « korr-kok » followed by a noisy wing flap, often at dawn.
fields.confusions: The very colourful male is hard to mix up. The brown female can look like a partridge, but her tail is much longer.
fields.anecdote: The Common Pheasant comes from Asia. It was brought to Europe centuries ago, mostly for hunting.
fields.hint: My very long tail trails behind me when I walk.

fields.summary: A small bird with a dark body and a reddish quivering tail. It is often perched on roofs and walls.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 23 to 26 cm, 14 to 20 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects on the ground or in short flights. It keeps shaking its reddish tail, as if to show where it is.
fields.why_here: It lives on cliffs, old walls, roofs and in towns or industrial areas that offer holes to nest in.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Some stay in winter, while others fly farther south and come back in March.
fields.by_ear: A creaky, unusual song with a part that sounds like crumpling paper or stirred gravel.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Common Redstart. But the male Black Redstart has no white forehead and no pale patches on the wing.
fields.anecdote: It was originally a bird of rocky cliffs. The Black Redstart has adapted perfectly to towns, where buildings copy its natural home.
fields.hint: I started on rocky cliffs and now live happily on city buildings.

fields.summary: A colourful small bird. The male has a white forehead, a black throat and an orange chest, and a quivering reddish tail.
fields.size: 13.5 cm long, wingspan 20 to 24 cm, 12 to 20 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects in short flights from a perch. It shakes its reddish tail all the time and nests in a tree hole.
fields.why_here: It lives in old broadleaf forests, orchards and parks with trees that have holes to nest in.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.by_ear: A short, flute-like song, starting with one clear note followed by creakier, varied phrases.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Black Redstart. But the male Common Redstart has a black throat, a white forehead and a much brighter orange belly.
fields.anecdote: Unlike the Black Redstart, which has adapted well to towns, the Common Redstart stays tied to woods with old trees.
fields.hint: A white spot decorates my forehead above a black throat.

fields.summary: A small, shy green-brown bird. It is one of the first migrants to come back in spring, known mostly by its very simple song.
fields.size: 11 cm long, wingspan 15 to 21 cm, 6 to 9 g
fields.behaviour: It eats tiny insects, which it hunts busily in the leaves, moving nonstop from branch to branch. It often wags its tail downward.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods, hedges, parks and gardens with trees and bushes, from sea level up to the mountains.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Many Common Chiffchaffs fly to southern Europe or North Africa in winter, but a growing number now spend the winter in France, especially on the coast.
fields.enemies: The stoat and the weasel can eat the eggs or chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A very simple, easy-to-know song, a dull repetition of two notes, « chiff-chaff ».
fields.confusions: It looks very much like the Willow Warbler and is almost impossible to tell apart without the song. The Common Chiffchaff has rather dark legs, while the Willow Warbler's are paler.
fields.anecdote: Its English name « chiffchaff » copies its song directly. It is one of the few birds whose common name truly matches its call.
fields.hint: My song always repeats the same two notes.

fields.summary: Very close to the Common Chiffchaff in looks, but you can know it by its falling, flute-like song. It is a long-distance migrant.
fields.size: 11 to 12.5 cm long, wingspan 17 to 22 cm, 7 to 13 g
fields.behaviour: It eats tiny insects in the leaves, very busy and always moving, like the Common Chiffchaff. It is usually more common in open places with birches or willows.
fields.why_here: It lives in light woods, bushy moors, riverbanks with willows and young forest areas, mostly during migration in France.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It crosses France in April or May on its way to nesting places farther north, and passes through again in August or September on its way to Africa south of the Sahara, where it spends winter.
fields.enemies: Cats and rats can eat its eggs. Jays, magpies and crows can attack the chicks.
fields.by_ear: A melodious, falling song, a cascade of clear, flute-like notes that slowly drop in pitch. It is very different from the dull song of the Common Chiffchaff.
fields.confusions: It looks almost the same as the Common Chiffchaff. The best way to tell them apart is the song. The Willow Warbler usually has paler legs.
fields.anecdote: Although it looks almost exactly like the Common Chiffchaff, it makes much longer migrations. Some birds reach southern Africa.
fields.hint: My song runs down a slope of clear notes.

fields.summary: A black and white crow-family bird with a long tail shining green and blue. It is easy to know and noisy.
fields.size: 44 to 46 cm long including a long tail, wingspan 52 to 60 cm, 200 to 250 g
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything it finds: insects, eggs, dead animals and scraps. It builds a big covered nest of sticks, often easy to see at the top of a lone tree.
fields.why_here: It lives in open countryside with scattered trees, in gardens and villages, where it finds varied food and good lookout spots.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year.
fields.enemies: The Carrion Crow can eat the eggs or chicks of the Eurasian Magpie.
fields.by_ear: A sharp, repeated call, a sort of fast rattle « tchac-tchac-tchac », easy to know from far away.
fields.confusions: It is hard to mix up thanks to its sharp black and white feathers and its typical long tail.
fields.anecdote: Despite a stubborn legend, the Magpie is not more drawn to shiny objects than other curious birds.
fields.hint: My black and white feathers hide blue-green shine.

fields.summary: A big woodpecker with olive-green feathers and a red cap. Unlike other woodpeckers, it spends a lot of time on the ground.
fields.size: 30 to 36 cm long, wingspan 45 to 51 cm, 150 to 220 g
fields.behaviour: It eats mostly ants, which it catches on the ground in anthills with its long, sticky tongue. So it spends much more time on the ground than other woodpeckers.
fields.why_here: It lives in meadows, orchards, parks and edges, with trees to nest in and grassy areas full of ants to feed on.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on the same territory and does not migrate.
fields.by_ear: A very easy-to-know call, a loud, rolling laugh that speeds up and then slows down. It is often compared to the whinny of a small horse.
fields.confusions: Its fully red cap and green feathers set it clearly apart from the other black and white woodpeckers in France. There is little risk of mix-up.
fields.anecdote: Its call, a loud, rolling laugh, gave it its French nickname « pivert ». Some people once believed it announced rain.
fields.hint: My call sounds like a loud, rolling laugh.

fields.summary: A small, shy brown tit with a shiny black cap and a black bib under the beak. Despite its name, it does not live in marshes.
fields.size: 11.5 cm long, wingspan 18 to 19.5 cm, 9 to 12 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for insects and seeds in bushes and undergrowth, often as a pair all year. It also hides seeds for later, like other tits.
fields.why_here: It lives in broadleaf woods with thick undergrowth, thick hedges and wooded gardens. It nests in a hole that it makes bigger itself in soft, rotting wood.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on the same territory and hardly moves.
fields.enemies: In nest boxes, the weasel, the Great Spotted Woodpecker and the Eurasian Jay can attack its chicks.
fields.by_ear: A special call, a nasal, explosive « pitchou » repeated, very useful for spotting it before seeing it. Its song is quieter, a series of repeated notes.
fields.confusions: It is very close to the Willow Tit, which is missing or rare in some regions. It is told apart mostly by the nasal « pitchou » call and the lack of a pale patch on the wing.
fields.anecdote: Despite a name that suggests marshes, it lives mostly in dry woods and gardens, never really near water.
fields.hint: I love dry woods; my call is a nasal « pitchou ».

fields.summary: A small, shy bird with streaky grey-brown feathers. It is often mixed up with a sparrow, though it is not from the same family.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 19 to 21 cm, 16 to 24 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds mostly on the ground, quietly under hedges, on insects and, in winter, small seeds. It hops along near the ground, rarely far from cover.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, thick hedges, undergrowth and scrub, where it finds both food and a hiding place. It nests low in a thick bush or a conifer hedge.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year, with some local or short-distance moves in winter, depending on the region.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk and cats can catch the adult Dunnock.
fields.by_ear: A smooth, hurried song, a high, steady twitter that is quite even, without the clear pauses of the European Robin. It is often sung from a low bush.
fields.confusions: From far away, it is often taken for a sparrow because of its dull brown feathers. But its beak is thin and pointed, unlike the short, cone-shaped beak of a sparrow.
fields.anecdote: Its shy ways and dull feathers make it one of the most underrated garden birds, even though it is often found under hedges.
fields.hint: People often mistake me for a sparrow.

fields.summary: A stocky, shy finch. The male has a bright pink-to-red breast and a black cap. The female is greyer with a touch of pink.
fields.size: 14.5 to 16.5 cm long, wingspan 22 to 26 cm, 21 to 27 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds, buds and berries, often moving quietly as a pair through bushes. It can damage fruit tree buds in spring.
fields.why_here: It lives in thick woods, thick hedges and gardens with dense bushes where it can hide. It often stays hidden despite its bright colours.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year. Sometimes a few birds from northern Europe arrive in hard winters.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. Jays and weasels can eat the eggs or chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A soft, flute-like contact call, a low, sad « dyoo » that is easy to know. Its quiet song carries little and is rarely heard.
fields.confusions: Its bright pink-red colour and clear black cap set it apart from every other songbird in France. There is little risk of a visual mix-up.
fields.anecdote: Despite its bright colours, it is a very shy bird. Often you first notice its soft call before you spot it in the thick leaves.
fields.hint: My breast is as pink as the spring flowers.

fields.summary: A cousin of the Goldcrest, just as tiny. You can know it by its white eyebrow and the black stripe through its eye.
fields.size: 9 to 10 cm long, wingspan 13 to 16 cm, 4 to 7 g
fields.behaviour: It eats tiny insects and spiders in the leaves, preferring conifers but also using broadleaf trees. Always on the move, it flits about nonstop.
fields.why_here: It lives in conifer forests as well as mixed woods and some gardens with dense trees. It is a bit less tied to conifers than the Goldcrest.
fields.migration: Some migrate in France. Some stay all year, while others move short distances south or to the Mediterranean coast in winter.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. Jays and magpies can attack the chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A high song close to the Goldcrest's but a bit more uneven and faster toward the end. Its contact call is also very high.
fields.confusions: It differs from the Goldcrest by its clear white eyebrow edged with black above the eye, which its cousin does not have.
fields.anecdote: Its French name refers to the three bands around its orange crown: two black and one white. It is a face pattern that is unique among European birds.
fields.hint: A white eyebrow underlines my bright eye.

fields.summary: One of the smallest birds in Europe. It is olive-green with a yellow and orange stripe on its head, and it lives with conifers.
fields.size: 9 cm long, wingspan 13.5 to 15.5 cm, 4.5 to 7 g
fields.behaviour: It eats tiny insects and spiders that it catches nonstop while flitting about in conifer needles. It is extremely busy and never stays still for long.
fields.why_here: It lives almost only in conifer forests and groves, where it finds food and thick branches to build a very hidden, hanging nest.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year, with local moves or small migrations depending on how hard the winter is and how much food there is.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adult Goldcrest.
fields.by_ear: An extremely high, fast song, a series of very thin notes that rise and then drop. It is often at the edge of what people can hear.
fields.confusions: It is very close to the Common Firecrest, but it lacks the black stripe through the eye. Its steadier song also helps tell them apart once you have learned it.
fields.anecdote: Despite its tiny size, barely heavier than a coin, it survives hard winters by sometimes huddling together in groups to save heat.
fields.hint: I weigh barely more than a big coin.

fields.summary: A small bird of moors. The male has a black head and an orange chest, and often perches in plain view.
fields.size: 12.5 cm long, wingspan 18 to 21 cm, 13 to 17 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects from a low perch, a bush or a wire, making short flights to catch its prey.
fields.why_here: It lives on moors, wasteland, bushy meadows and banks, where it finds low perches and insects.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Some stay in winter, while others fly farther south and come back as early as February or March.
fields.enemies: The Red Fox can eat its eggs or chicks in the nest on the ground.
fields.by_ear: A sharp call like two stones knocking together, « tac-tac », which gave the bird its name.
fields.confusions: It can be mixed up with the Whinchat, which is rarer and has a clear white eyebrow that the European Stonechat does not have.
fields.anecdote: The French name « pâtre », which means shepherd, may come from its habit of perching near herds in pastures to hunt the insects they stir up.
fields.hint: I dart from a low perch to catch insects.

fields.summary: A tiny, bright yellow finch, the smallest finch in Europe. It is often heard before it is seen, thanks to its creaky song.
fields.size: 11.5 cm long, wingspan 20 to 23 cm, 10 to 14 g
fields.behaviour: It eats small seeds on the ground and in grass, moving in quick little hops. It often perches in plain view at the top of a tree or an aerial to sing.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks, orchards and village edges in the warmer parts of France, with trees to nest in and open ground to feed on.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Many serins leave France in autumn for Spain and North Africa and come back in spring, though some stay all year in the south.
fields.by_ear: A very fast, creaky song, a sort of nonstop, shrill crackle like a little bell, given without a pause from a high perch.
fields.confusions: From far away, it can be mixed up with a young Greenfinch. But its small size and special creaky song help you know it.
fields.anecdote: Its crackling, nonstop song has been compared to the sound of a little bell or a bicycle bell being shaken endlessly.
fields.hint: My song sounds like the creak of a tiny bell.

fields.summary: A stocky bird with a blue-grey back and an orange belly. It is famous for being the only bird that can walk down tree trunks head first.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 22.5 to 27 cm, 17 to 28 g
fields.behaviour: It climbs up and down tree trunks in every direction, looking for insects hidden under the bark. It cracks seeds wedged in crevices with its beak. It also hides food for later.
fields.why_here: It lives in old broadleaf woods, parks and big gardens with old trees that offer holes to nest in.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year, faithful to its wooded territory, and hardly moves.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk hunts the adult Eurasian Nuthatch.
fields.by_ear: A strong, loud call, a clear, repeated « pwi-pwi-pwi », or a fast, strong trill, much louder than you would expect from its small size.
fields.confusions: Its special ability to go down trunks head first, unlike woodpeckers, which never do, makes it easy to know.
fields.anecdote: It makes the entrance of its nest hole smaller by plastering it with dried mud, to stop bigger rivals from getting in. That gave it its French name « torchepot », which refers to plastering.
fields.hint: I walk down tree trunks head first.

fields.summary: A small, very busy yellow-green and black finch. In winter, it lives in acrobatic groups hanging on alder and birch cones.
fields.size: 12 cm long, wingspan 20 to 23 cm, 10 to 18 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds in flocks, often hanging upside down at the ends of branches to pull seeds from alder and birch cones. It is very sociable outside the breeding season.
fields.why_here: In winter, it lives in alder and birch groves and in gardens with feeders, especially near streams where alders grow. It nests more rarely in France, mostly in the mountains.
fields.migration: It is a migrant and an irregular winter visitor in France. Numbers change a lot from one winter to the next, depending on how many seeds there are in northern Europe.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adult Eurasian Siskin.
fields.by_ear: A nasal, musical flight call, often given by a tight group moving fast from tree to tree. Its twittering, varied song is heard more rarely in France.
fields.confusions: The male, with his black cap, can look like a young goldfinch. But he is more yellow-green, with no red and no black and white pattern on the head.
fields.anecdote: Its winter arrivals in France can change hugely from one year to the next, depending on the conifer seed crop in northern Europe.
fields.hint: I hang upside down to eat.

fields.summary: A pale pinkish-beige dove with a thin black collar on the back of the neck. It has been very common near homes since arriving in Europe in the 20th century.
fields.size: 31 to 33 cm long, wingspan 47 to 55 cm, 150 to 220 g
fields.behaviour: It eats seeds on the ground, often near feeders or farm grain stores. It flies straight, with fast, stiff wingbeats.
fields.why_here: It is closely tied to places where people live, such as gardens, villages and towns. There it finds food and nesting spots in trees close to houses.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year in the same area, with no real migration.
fields.enemies: Magpies, jays and crows can eat its eggs or chicks.
fields.by_ear: A simple, dull song, three syllables repeated again and again, « coo-COO-coo », often heard nonstop from a wire or a roof.
fields.confusions: The European Turtle Dove has redder, scaly feathers with no full black collar, and a more purring song. The Eurasian Collared Dove has a clear black collar and paler, more even feathers.
fields.anecdote: It comes from Asia and the Balkans. It spread across all of Europe in a few decades in the 20th century, one of the fastest spreads ever seen in a bird.
fields.hint: I came from Asia and spread across Europe in decades.

fields.summary: A small, shy dove with reddish, scaly feathers. Its numbers have fallen sharply in Europe in recent decades.
fields.size: 26 to 28 cm long, wingspan 47 to 53 cm, 130 to 180 g
fields.behaviour: It eats small seeds of wild plants on the ground. It is shy and wary compared with the Eurasian Collared Dove. It flies fast with sharp wingbeats.
fields.why_here: It lives in hedgerows, light woods and farm edges, with thick bushes to nest in and grassy areas full of wild seeds.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and leaves as early as August or September to spend winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.by_ear: A soft, purring song, a series of repeated, cooing « rrrou-rrrou ». It is deeper and softer than the Eurasian Collared Dove's dull song.
fields.confusions: It differs from the Eurasian Collared Dove by its reddish, scaly back and by having no full black collar. Instead it has thin black and white stripes on the side of the neck.
fields.anecdote: Its numbers have dropped dramatically in Europe since the 1980s, partly because hedges have disappeared and it is hunted along its migration route.
fields.hint: My back has reddish scales.

fields.summary: The most common owl in France. It has spotted brown feathers and a big round head with no feather tufts. It is active mostly at night.
fields.size: 37 to 39 cm long, wingspan 94 to 104 cm, 330 to 590 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts at night, mostly small rodents like mice, which it finds with extremely sharp hearing. Its flight is silent thanks to special feathers that muffle the sound of its wings.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods, parks and big gardens with old trees that have holes to nest in, even in towns if old enough trees are there.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its night-time territory and does not migrate.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Eagle-Owl and the Northern Goshawk can catch the adults. Foxes can catch young birds that have just left the nest.
fields.by_ear: A very well-known night song, a long, trembling, sad hoot, often written as « hoo-hoo-hoohoohoo », typical of forest nights.
fields.confusions: The female's sharp « kewick » call, often heard apart from the male's hoot, is sometimes wrongly taken for the call of another species.
fields.anecdote: Its flight is almost totally silent thanks to the special edge of its feathers. That lets it surprise prey in total darkness.
fields.hint: My night flight makes almost no sound.

fields.summary: A small black bird with a green and purple shine, spotted with white in winter. It is very sociable.
fields.size: 20 to 22 cm long, wingspan 37 to 42 cm, 60 to 96 g
fields.behaviour: It eats almost anything: insects and fruit on the ground. It forms huge, spectacular flocks, mostly at the end of the day in winter, before landing to sleep.
fields.why_here: It lives in meadows, towns and countryside, where it finds insects on the ground and holes to nest in, including in buildings.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. In winter, many more arrive from northern and eastern Europe.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A very varied song, a mix of whistles, clicks and copies of other birds, or even machine noises.
fields.confusions: From far away, it can be mixed up with a blackbird. But its faster, more direct flight and stocky shape tell them apart easily.
fields.anecdote: The Common Starling is an excellent mimic. It can copy the songs of other birds and many sounds around it.
fields.hint: In winter, thousands of us draw clouds in the sky.

fields.summary: A small grey warbler. The male has a black cap and the female a reddish-brown cap. It is famous for its flute-like song.
fields.size: 13.5 cm long, wingspan 20 to 23 cm, 15 to 22 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects in summer and turns to berries in autumn and winter, especially ivy berries. It moves mostly in thick leaves and stays hidden despite its song.
fields.why_here: It lives in wooded gardens, hedges, undergrowth and parks with thick bushes to nest in and berries for winter.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Most French Eurasian Blackcaps fly to southern Europe or North Africa in winter, but a growing number now spend winter in France thanks to feeders.
fields.enemies: Cats and the Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A flute-like, melodious song. It starts with a quiet twitter, then rises into clear, whistled phrases that get louder and louder. It is very pleasant to hear.
fields.confusions: It differs from the Garden Warbler, which has plain brown feathers with no coloured cap, by its clear black or reddish cap.
fields.anecdote: More and more Eurasian Blackcaps choose to spend winter in France instead of Africa. This change in behaviour is partly linked to garden feeders.
fields.hint: I hide in thick leaves, and in winter I eat ivy berries.

fields.summary: A warbler with plain olive-brown feathers and no clear marks. It is often called the shyest of its group.
fields.size: 14 cm long, wingspan 20 to 24 cm, 17 to 25 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects in thick leaves in summer, then berries to fatten up before migration. It stays very hidden in thick plants.
fields.why_here: It lives in thick undergrowth, thick hedges and gardens with dense bushes, where it can hide easily despite a rather loud song.
fields.migration: It is a long-distance migrant. It arrives in France in April or May and leaves as early as August or September to spend winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk and cats hunt the Garden Warbler.
fields.by_ear: A smooth, nonstop song, one long musical phrase with no clear pause. It is softer and less flute-like than the Eurasian Blackcap's.
fields.confusions: Its total lack of marks on the head, unlike the Eurasian Blackcap, is exactly its main clue.
fields.anecdote: Its plain, shy look makes it a challenge for beginners, who often learn to know it first by its song rather than by sight.
fields.hint: Nothing really sets my head apart from the rest of my body.

fields.summary: The smallest grebe in Europe, plump and reddish-brown. It dives all the time and often vanishes under the water.
fields.size: 25 to 29 cm long, wingspan 40 to 45 cm, 100 to 230 g
fields.behaviour: It dives often to catch small fish and water animals without backbones. It stays very hidden, preferring to hide in plants.
fields.why_here: It lives at small ponds, pools and calm streams with thick plants along the edge to hide in.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Some move south or to the coast when the water freezes.
fields.by_ear: A loud, trilling call, a high, fast whinny that is easy to know despite the bird's small size.
fields.confusions: From far away, it can be mixed up with a young duck or a coot. But its small round shape and frequent diving tell it apart.
fields.anecdote: The Little Grebe can vanish under the water in an instant and come back up far from where it dived. This often puzzles people watching it.
fields.hint: Round and plump, I vanish under the water in a blink.

fields.summary: A tiny, plump brown bird with a tail held up. It is one of the smallest in Europe, yet has a surprisingly powerful song.
fields.size: 9 to 10 cm long, wingspan 13 to 17 cm, 7 to 12 g
fields.behaviour: It slips through bushes, wood piles and ivy near the ground, looking for tiny insects and spiders. It is very shy despite its strong song.
fields.why_here: It lives in thick undergrowth, hedges and gardens with ivy or piles of branches, where it finds shelter and food all year.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year. Very hard winters can wipe out local groups, but they recover fast.
fields.enemies: Cats and foxes can catch it.
fields.by_ear: A song that is extremely strong for its size, a fast cascade of high notes and trills, often ending with a vibrating roll. It can be heard from very far away.
fields.confusions: Its tiny size and its tail held straight up make it easy to tell from any other garden bird, despite its plain brown feathers.
fields.anecdote: For its size, its song is one of the strongest in the animal world. Relatively, it is as loud as a rooster crowing.
fields.hint: I hold my tiny tail straight up.

fields.summary: A big, all-black bird, with a bright orange beak in the male. The female is more brown. It is one of the most melodious singers in gardens.
fields.size: 24 to 25 cm long, wingspan 34 to 38.5 cm, 80 to 125 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for earthworms and insects on the ground, hopping and then stopping short with its head tilted, listening. It also happily eats fruit and berries. It can be shy or very close to people in towns.
fields.why_here: It lives in gardens, parks, hedges and forest edges, anywhere it finds lawns and bushes to nest in. It builds its nest low, in a thick hedge or a shrub.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year. Some birds from northern Europe come here in winter to enjoy a milder climate.
fields.enemies: Cats and the Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. Cats also catch the young that have just left the nest.
fields.by_ear: A rich, flute-like, calm song, sung mostly at dawn and dusk from a high spot like a roof. Its typical alarm call is a sharp, fast « tchac-tchac-tchac » at sunset.
fields.confusions: The Common Starling is stockier, with speckled, shiny feathers and a more direct flight. The brown female can look like a thrush, but she has no evenly spotted chest.
fields.anecdote: In towns, some blackbirds have changed their song so that it can be heard over the noise of traffic.
fields.hint: My beak is brighter than all my feathers.

fields.summary: A spotted brown bird, a smaller, slimmer cousin of the Mistle Thrush. It is known for its very repetitive, powerful song.
fields.size: 20 to 22 cm long, wingspan 33 to 36 cm, 50 to 107 g
fields.behaviour: It looks for insects, worms and above all snails on the ground. It breaks the shells by hitting them on a stone called an « anvil ». It moves in hops on lawns and under hedges.
fields.why_here: It lives in wooded gardens, parks, hedges and forest edges with thick undergrowth to nest in. It needs stones or hard surfaces nearby to open snails.
fields.migration: Some migrate. Some leave France in autumn for Spain or North Africa, while others stay or arrive from the north for winter.
fields.enemies: Cats and sparrowhawks can catch the adults. Magpies and jays can eat the eggs or chicks.
fields.by_ear: A very easy-to-know song of short phrases repeated three or four times in a row before changing, as if the bird were trying out several ideas. It is loud, often sung from the top of a tree.
fields.confusions: It differs from the Mistle Thrush by its smaller size and repeating song. The Mistle Thrush sings long phrases that are not repeated. Its spotted feathers also look like a young starling's.
fields.anecdote: It always uses the same stone as an anvil. Sometimes you can find a little pile of broken snail shells there.
fields.hint: I repeat each phrase three or four times, then change.

fields.summary: A big, sociable thrush with a grey head and a reddish-brown back. It travels and feeds in noisy flocks, mostly in winter.
fields.size: 25 cm long, wingspan 39 to 42 cm, 80 to 140 g
fields.behaviour: It feeds in flocks in meadows and orchards, on the ground, on worms and insects, then on berries in winter, especially hawthorn or fallen apples. It is very sociable and noisy in flight.
fields.why_here: It looks for open meadows, orchards and hedges full of berries, mostly in winter. In France, it nests mostly in the east and north-east, in light groves.
fields.migration: It is a migrant and winter visitor. Most Fieldfares seen in France in winter come from northern and eastern Europe. They arrive in October or November and leave in March.
fields.enemies: The Eurasian Sparrowhawk can catch the adults. The stoat can eat the eggs or chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A typical flight call, a sharp, chattering « tchac-tchac-tchac » given in a group. It is often the first sign it is there, before you even see it.
fields.confusions: Its grey head and reddish back set it clearly apart from other thrushes, which are more evenly brown. In a noisy flock in flight, it can look like a starling, but it is bigger.
fields.anecdote: It travels in flocks that can number several hundred birds, moving together from one orchard to another all winter.
fields.hint: I travel in noisy, chattering flocks in winter.

fields.summary: The biggest thrush in Europe, with spotted feathers and a sturdy look. It often perches in plain view at the top of a tree.
fields.size: 27 cm long, wingspan 42 to 48 cm, 100 to 160 g
fields.behaviour: It eats worms, insects and especially mistletoe berries, which it defends fiercely against other birds in winter. It flies in strong, wavy lines.
fields.why_here: It lives in big parks, light woods and orchards with old trees, especially ones with mistletoe. It nests high, in the fork of a big branch.
fields.migration: It mostly stays in France all year, with some local moves in winter depending on berries.
fields.enemies: Birds of prey can catch the adults. Cats can eat the eggs or chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A loud, sad song in short, spaced phrases, often sung from the top of a big tree even in rain or wind. That is why it is nicknamed the « storm bird ».
fields.confusions: It is bigger and greyer than the Song Thrush, with a song of phrases that are not repeated. It can be mixed up with a young, spotted blackbird, which is smaller and darker.
fields.anecdote: It is sometimes nicknamed the « storm bird » because it keeps singing even in rain and wind, when other birds fall silent.
fields.hint: I sing even when the wind blows hard.

fields.summary: A night bird of prey with pale feathers and a white, heart-shaped face. It is typical of old buildings and church towers, where it has long found shelter.
fields.size: 33 to 39 cm long, wingspan 85 to 93 cm, 187 to 490 g
fields.behaviour: It hunts at night over meadows and fields, mainly small rodents like voles, which it finds with outstanding hearing. Its flight is silent and low over the grass.
fields.why_here: It lives in open farmland with meadows to hunt in, and old buildings, barns or church towers to nest and perch in.
fields.migration: It stays in France all year on its territory, though numbers can drop sharply after very hard winters.
fields.by_ear: A very easy-to-know call, a long, hoarse, rasping screech, very different from the hooting of the Tawny Owl.
fields.confusions: Its white, heart-shaped face and pale feathers, almost white underneath, set it clearly apart from the Tawny Owl, which is browner and has no heart-shaped face.
fields.anecdote: Its disc-shaped face works like a satellite dish, gathering sounds toward its ears. That lets it find prey in total darkness by hearing alone.
fields.hint: My face makes a heart, all white.

fields.summary: A spectacular orange bird with a long, upright crest and black and white wings, and a long, thin, curved beak.
fields.size: 26 to 28 cm long, wingspan 44 to 48 cm, 55 to 80 g
fields.behaviour: It probes the ground with its long beak to catch grubs and insects. It spreads its crest like a fan when it is alarmed or excited.
fields.why_here: It lives in orchards, dry meadows, vineyards and open places with soft soil where it probes for prey.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It arrives in France in March or April and flies back to Africa south of the Sahara in August or September.
fields.enemies: The Peregrine Falcon can catch it. Grass snakes can eat the chicks in the nest.
fields.by_ear: A very easy-to-know song, a dull, repeated « hoo-hoo-hoo » that gave the bird its name.
fields.confusions: Few birds can be mixed up with it, thanks to its shape and colours, which are unique in Europe.
fields.anecdote: Its name comes straight from its typical call, repeated again and again in spring.
fields.hint: My crest opens like a fan on my head.

fields.summary: A farmland bird with black and white feathers shining green, topped with a thin crest that curls backward.
fields.size: 28 to 31 cm long, wingspan 82 to 87 cm, 150 to 300 g
fields.behaviour: It eats insects and worms on the ground in fields. In spring, it does spectacular acrobatic display flights.
fields.why_here: It lives in wet meadows, ploughed fields and open farmland, where it nests right on the ground.
fields.migration: Some stay in France all year. Birds from the north come to spend the winter in big groups, from October to March.
fields.enemies: Crows, gulls and stoats can eat its eggs.
fields.by_ear: A nasal, sad call, put into words as « pee-wit », often given during acrobatic display flights.
fields.confusions: Few birds can be mixed up with it, thanks to its thin curled crest and its typical shiny black and white feathers.
fields.anecdote: The Northern Lapwing sometimes pretends to be hurt, dragging a wing on the ground to lead a predator away from its nest or chicks.
fields.hint: A thin, curled crest decorates the top of my head.

fields.summary: The Red Junglefowl is a wild bird from Asia and an ancestor of our farm chickens. The male has a red comb and a long, curved tail.
fields.behaviour: It scratches the ground to find seeds, small fruit and insects. It goes to a perch to sleep, safe from the ground.
fields.why_here: Its natural home is in forests and their edges in Asia. In France, a call linked to this name may come from a farm bird.
fields.migration: It is not a usual wild migrant in France. Farm birds can be heard all year.
fields.by_ear: The male gives a loud rooster crow. Sound alone cannot tell you that a wild bird is there.
fields.confusions: Farm roosters can make very similar calls. So the setting, such as a farmyard, is key.
fields.anecdote: The chickens on our farms come in part from this wild species.
fields.hint: I scratch the ground and sleep perched in trees.

fields.summary: The Peregrine Falcon is a bird of prey with pointed wings that hunts mostly birds in open sky. Its dark head has wide black marks under the eyes.
fields.behaviour: It watches from a high spot, then chases its prey in flight. It can attack by diving suddenly from the sky.
fields.why_here: Cliffs give it nesting places. In towns, some buildings give it similar ledges, near birds to hunt.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in France. Birds from farther north join the local birds in the cold season.
fields.by_ear: Near the nest, its alarm calls are sharp and repeated. Its hunting flight can stay silent.
fields.confusions: The Eurasian Hobby is smaller and slimmer. The adult has reddish feathers under the tail and on the legs, which the Peregrine Falcon does not have.
fields.anecdote: A skyscraper can serve as a cliff for raising its chicks.
fields.hint: My black moustaches frame a hunter's gaze.

fields.summary: The Common Sandpiper is a small bird of riverbanks. Its brown back stands out from its white belly, and its rear end bobs as it walks.
fields.behaviour: It picks small animals at the water's edge. When disturbed, it shoots low over the surface with quick wingbeats.
fields.why_here: Stony shores, small islands and open edges of water give it food and places to hide.
fields.migration: It passes through France during migration and nests here in some places. Some stay in winter, so you can see it in different seasons.
fields.by_ear: Its call is a short series of high, whistled notes, often given as it takes off.
fields.confusions: The Green Sandpiper shows a more striking white rump in flight. The Common Sandpiper has a white wedge of belly in front of its folded wing.
fields.anecdote: Its repeated bobbing helps you spot it even when its feathers blend in with the pebbles.
fields.hint: I bob my rear end by the water.

fields.summary: The Northern Wheatear is a small bird of open places. When it flies off, its white tail with a black T becomes very easy to see.
fields.behaviour: It watches the ground from a stone or a clod of earth, then drops down to catch insects. It often stands tall to look around.
fields.why_here: It looks for open ground with short plants, with stones, holes or small bumps. During migration, it may stop in fields.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It passes through France in spring and autumn. Some nest in the country, then fly to Africa for winter.
fields.by_ear: Its song mixes short, whistled phrases and rougher sounds. Its small, sharp calls can go with tail movements.
fields.confusions: Chats also perch in the open. The black T on the Northern Wheatear's white tail is an especially useful clue.
fields.anecdote: Its nest can be hidden in a hole in the ground or between stones.
fields.hint: My white tail draws a black T when I take off.

fields.summary: The Sand Martin is a small brown swallow with a white belly and a brown band across the chest. It nests in groups in soft banks.
fields.behaviour: It hunts insects in flight, often over water. Pairs dig tunnels where they build their nest.
fields.why_here: Sandy riverbanks and quarry faces give it walls to nest in. Nearby wet places attract its prey.
fields.migration: It comes back to France in the warm season and flies to Africa after breeding. Groups stop over during migration.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are short, sharp and a little rasping. Around a colony, many birds answer each other nonstop.
fields.confusions: The Western House Martin has a white rump and a dark top. The Sand Martin has a brown back and a brown chest band.
fields.anecdote: The nest is at the end of a tunnel dug in a bank.
fields.hint: My bedroom is at the end of a tunnel I dig myself.

fields.summary: The Redwing is a small thrush with a pale eyebrow and reddish flanks. It visits France mostly in the cold season.
fields.behaviour: It looks for worms and other small animals on the ground. In autumn and winter, it also eats berries, often in a group.
fields.why_here: Hedges full of fruit, meadows and edges give it food during its winter stay.
fields.migration: It arrives mostly in autumn from its breeding areas farther north and leaves in spring. You can also hear it during its night flights.
fields.by_ear: On night migration, it gives a thin, drawn-out whistle. On a calm night, you can sometimes hear it without seeing the bird.
fields.confusions: The Song Thrush does not have its wide pale eyebrow or its reddish flanks. These two marks are useful when the bird is perched.
fields.anecdote: Migrants can pass over a town while its people sleep.
fields.hint: I fly over towns at night while people sleep, whistling thinly.

fields.summary: The European Pied Flycatcher is a small insect hunter. The male in breeding feathers often shows a black and white contrast, while the female is browner.
fields.behaviour: It watches from a branch, darts at an insect, then goes back to perch. It also picks prey from leaves.
fields.why_here: It lives in woods and tree-filled parks. To nest, it looks for a tree hole or a suitable nest box.
fields.migration: It is a migrant. It stays in France in the warm season or stops over on its way. It spends winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
fields.by_ear: Its song is made of little rhythmic phrases, with repeated clear notes. Its contact calls are short.
fields.confusions: The Spotted Flycatcher has a finely streaked chest and looks less contrasting. Brown females need more care.
fields.anecdote: It can build its nest in an old woodpecker hole.
fields.hint: I may nest in an old woodpecker hole.

fields.summary: The Western Marsh Harrier is a bird of prey of marshes. Its long wings held up in a V help it patrol slowly over the plants.
fields.behaviour: It flies over reeds and meadows to surprise small animals. It usually nests in tall, thick plants.
fields.why_here: Reedbeds give it shelter for its nest. Nearby marshes, fields and meadows are its hunting grounds.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in some parts of France. Some birds migrate, while others stay or come to spend the winter.
fields.by_ear: Its calls near the nest are high and whistled. When hunting, it is often quiet to the ear.
fields.confusions: The Common Buzzard has a more compact shape and often glides in circles. The Western Marsh Harrier likes to patrol low on long wings.
fields.anecdote: Partners can pass food to each other in mid-air.

fields.summary: The Osprey is a bird of prey that specialises in fishing. Its pale underside and the dark band across its eye help you know it.
fields.behaviour: It watches the water in flight, then dives feet first to grab a fish. It carries its catch to a perch.
fields.why_here: Lakes, ponds, rivers and coasts give it fish. To nest, it uses a high, open spot, often a big tree.
fields.migration: You see it mostly during migration and in the warm season in France. A few birds also spend winter here, though not all stay all year.
fields.by_ear: It gives high whistles, often repeated near the nest or when meeting another bird.
fields.confusions: Big gulls do not have its talons or its dark eye mask. In flight, its bird-of-prey shape has long, bent wings.
fields.anecdote: It can turn its fish head first while carrying it.
fields.hint: I dive feet first to carry off a fish.

fields.summary: The Brambling visits France mostly in winter. It has an orange breast, a pale belly and a white rump that is easy to see as it takes off.
fields.behaviour: It looks for seeds on the ground, especially in beech woods. Birds can gather to feed and to spend the night.
fields.why_here: Beech forests, fields and sometimes gardens give it seeds in the cold season.
fields.migration: It arrives from northern Europe in autumn and leaves in spring. Its numbers change from year to year with the food available.
fields.by_ear: Its calls have a nasal, slightly rasping sound, different from the cleaner notes of the Eurasian Chaffinch.
fields.confusions: The Eurasian Chaffinch does not have its white rump. In the Brambling, the orange breast stands out against the pale belly.
fields.anecdote: A big crop of beech nuts can attract huge gatherings.
fields.hint: My white rump shines when the flock takes off.

fields.summary: The European Honey Buzzard looks like a buzzard, but its small head gives it a special shape. It looks mostly for wasp and bumblebee grubs.
fields.behaviour: It finds their nests and scratches the ground to reach the grubs. It also eats other small animals.
fields.why_here: Forests give it trees to nest in. Clearings, meadows and edges let it look for the insects it feeds on.
fields.migration: It comes back to France in spring to breed and flies to Africa at the end of the warm season.
fields.by_ear: Its call is a fairly thin, drawn-out whistle. It is often silent, even when gliding above the trees.
fields.confusions: The Common Buzzard usually has a stronger head and a shorter tail. The European Honey Buzzard's feathers vary a lot, so they are not enough on their own.
fields.anecdote: The tight feathers on its face help protect it when it digs into wasp nests.
fields.hint: I dig up nests to eat wasp grubs.

fields.summary: The Lesser Black-backed Gull is a big seabird with a dark back. In adults, yellow legs stand out against the white belly.
fields.behaviour: It looks for fish, small animals and leftover food. It also feeds on land and can follow people at work.
fields.why_here: It likes coasts, river mouths and some inland lakes. Fields or towns can also give it food.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in France, but many birds travel between their breeding and wintering places.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are loud and varied. Telling the big gulls apart by ear alone is tricky.
fields.confusions: The Great Black-backed Gull is bulkier and has pink legs. The adult Lesser Black-backed Gull has yellow legs and a slimmer shape.
fields.anecdote: It can look for food far from the sea, even on farmland.
fields.hint: I look for food far from the sea, even on farmland.

fields.summary: The Eurasian Hobby is a slim bird of prey with long, pointed wings. The adult has rusty feathers on its upper legs and under its tail.
fields.behaviour: It catches big insects and small birds in flight. It can eat an insect while still flying.
fields.why_here: Open country near woods and wetlands gives it perches, nest sites and flying prey.
fields.migration: It comes back to France in the warm season to breed and flies off to Africa after summer.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are high, repeated notes, mostly near the nest. Its chases in the air can happen without a sound.
fields.confusions: The Peregrine Falcon is more powerful. Long, slim wings and rusty feathers under the body mark the adult Eurasian Hobby.
fields.anecdote: It often uses an old crow-family nest instead of building one.
fields.hint: Sometimes I snack on a dragonfly without stopping my flight.

fields.summary: The Common Tern is a pale bird with slim wings and a forked tail. It dives to fish and often nests in colonies.
fields.behaviour: It flies over the water, hovers for a moment, then dives to grab a small fish. Partners sometimes offer each other fish during courtship.
fields.why_here: It looks for waters full of fish and open spots to nest, like islets, sandbanks or floating rafts built for it.
fields.migration: It is a migrant: it comes back to France in spring and leaves after breeding. You can see birds passing on coasts and near inland waters.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are piercing, often drawn out and grating. A colony can be very noisy when an intruder comes close.
fields.confusions: The Arctic Tern looks very much like it. You must check the leg length, the bill and the wing details carefully.
fields.anecdote: A floating raft can become a nesting island.
fields.hint: I dive like an arrow above a noisy islet.

fields.summary: The Common Quail is a small, round, brown bird that hides in the grass. You often hear the male before you see him.
fields.behaviour: It walks through plants and eats seeds and small animals. It prefers to hide or run rather than fly away.
fields.why_here: Meadows and crops with plant cover give it food and a hidden nest on the ground.
fields.migration: It is a migrant, mostly found in France in the warm season. Where and when it appears depends on the region and the conditions.
fields.by_ear: The male repeats a short, rhythmic pattern, often written as « paie tes dettes » ("pay your debts"). The song sometimes comes from a seemingly empty field.
fields.confusions: The Grey Partridge is much bigger and sturdier. A recorded call is not enough to tell apart every farm-raised bird.
fields.anecdote: Despite its round shape and walking habits, it makes real migrations.
fields.hint: My rhythmic song comes from a field where I hide.

fields.summary: The Black Tern is a small wetland bird. In breeding plumage, its dark head and body stand out against its grey wings.
fields.behaviour: It flies low over water and plants to catch insects. It also picks small water animals from the surface.
fields.why_here: Marshes and lakes rich in insects give it places to rest. The few breeding sites have the right water plants.
fields.migration: It is a migrant: it crosses France and nests here in only a few places in the warm season. It leaves for winter further south.
fields.by_ear: It makes small, short, rasping calls, mostly when birds talk to each other.
fields.confusions: The adult Whiskered Tern keeps white cheeks under a black cap. The Black Tern in breeding plumage has an all-dark head.
fields.anecdote: Its nest can sit on the floating plants of a marsh.
fields.hint: In the warm season, my head turns all dark.

fields.summary: The Common Greenshank is a slender shorebird with a slightly upturned bill. Its long legs have a greenish tint.
fields.behaviour: It wades in shallow water to catch small animals. It can run after fish in puddles.
fields.why_here: Mudflats, lagoons and pond edges give it shallow water and easy prey.
fields.migration: It crosses France during migration and can also spend the winter here. So birds do not always stay in the same place all year.
fields.by_ear: Its loud call is often a short run of clear, whistled, slightly sad notes.
fields.confusions: The Common Redshank has red legs. The Common Greenshank has a slightly upturned bill and duller legs.
fields.anecdote: It does not just peck: it can actively chase a small fish.
fields.hint: I run after little fish in shallow puddles.

fields.summary: The Wood Sandpiper is a small bird of shallow waters. A pale eyebrow marks its eye, above a brown back with speckles.
fields.behaviour: It walks in water or on mud and picks up small animals. It likes wetlands during its travels.
fields.why_here: Marshes, flooded meadows and pond edges give it feeding stops, mostly in fresh water.
fields.migration: You see it in France mainly during spring migration and in late summer. It keeps going to its African winter homes.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are thin and repeated, with a clear, quick sound.
fields.confusions: The Green Sandpiper looks darker on top. The Wood Sandpiper has a more visible eyebrow and a paler underwing.
fields.anecdote: A meadow that is flooded for a while can become a useful stop on its journey.
fields.hint: My pale eyebrow stands out in flooded meadows.

fields.summary: The Whinchat is a small bird with a wide pale eyebrow. It likes to perch on top of a stem to watch over the meadow.
fields.behaviour: From its perch, it spots insects and catches them on the ground or in the air. Its nest is hidden in plants on the ground.
fields.why_here: Meadows full of insects and dotted with tall stems give it food, lookout posts and places to nest.
fields.migration: It comes back to France in spring and leaves for Africa after breeding. Some migrants also stop here on their way.
fields.by_ear: Its song is a short run of varied notes, sometimes rough. Its alarm calls mix short, dry sounds.
fields.confusions: The European Stonechat has no wide pale eyebrow. The Whinchat also shows white at the base of its tail in flight.
fields.anecdote: A simple dry stem can serve as its lookout post.
fields.hint: From a stem, my wide pale eyebrow watches over the meadow.

fields.summary: The Common Ringed Plover is a small bird of beaches and shores. The adult has a black collar and a short bill that is often orange at the base.
fields.behaviour: It runs a few steps, stops, then pecks at a small prey. Its frequent stops make its feeding easy to follow.
fields.why_here: Bare sand, mud and pebbles let it feed. Quiet beaches can also hold its nest on the ground.
fields.migration: You can see it in France in different seasons. Local nesters share the shore with migrants and winter visitors, depending on the time of year.
fields.by_ear: It gives fairly soft whistled calls, often when taking off or to stay in touch.
fields.confusions: The Little Ringed Plover has a yellow ring around the eye. The adult Common Ringed Plover has orange legs and a white wing bar in flight.
fields.anecdote: Its eggs blend in with the small stones on the ground.
fields.hint: I run, I stop, then I peck among the pebbles.

fields.summary: The Little Ringed Plover is a small bird with a black collar. Its bright yellow ring around the eye stands out when you see it up close.
fields.behaviour: It switches between short runs and pauses to catch insects and other tiny animals. The nest is just a dip in the ground.
fields.why_here: River shores, pebble islands and some quarries give it bare ground to feed and nest.
fields.migration: It comes back to France in the warm season and usually leaves its breeding sites before winter. Migration also brings passing birds.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are high, short and whistled, especially when it takes off.
fields.confusions: The Common Ringed Plover does not have such a strong yellow ring. The Little Ringed Plover has an all-dark bill.
fields.anecdote: It can nest on freshly turned ground, as long as the soil stays bare.
fields.hint: My nest is just a hollow in bare ground.

fields.summary: The adult Mediterranean Gull has a black hood in summer and very white wings. Its red bill is fairly thick.
fields.behaviour: It looks for small animals in fields, wetlands and on the coast. It nests in colonies.
fields.why_here: Islets and wetlands offer places to breed. Meadows and coasts give it food.
fields.migration: You can see it in France all year, with trips between breeding and wintering places. The birds present change with the season.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are loud and nasal, deeper than its shape would make you expect.
fields.confusions: The Black-headed Gull has black wingtips. On the adult Mediterranean Gull, the wings look white all the way to the end.
fields.anecdote: The black summer hood mostly disappears in winter plumage.
fields.hint: As an adult, my wings stay white right to the tips.

fields.summary: The Merlin is a small, fast bird of prey of open spaces. Its compact shape goes with a flight that is often low and direct.
fields.behaviour: It mostly chases small birds, sometimes just above the ground. It uses a clod of earth or a post as a lookout.
fields.why_here: Plains, marshes and coastal flats give it space to hunt small birds.
fields.migration: You find it in France mostly in the cold season and during migration. It breeds mainly in regions further north.
fields.by_ear: It is often silent during its winter stay. So identifying it by sound alone needs care.
fields.confusions: The Common Kestrel often hovers in place to look for food. The Merlin hunts more with fast, low chases.
fields.anecdote: Its small size does not stop it from chasing birds in mid-air.
fields.hint: A compact little raptor, I chase birds just above the ground.

fields.summary: The Northern Raven is a big black bird with a powerful bill. In flight, its tail has a very typical wedge shape.
fields.behaviour: It eats very varied food, from small animals to leftovers from dead animals. Pairs can perform games in the air.
fields.why_here: Cliffs, mountains and big woods give it nest sites. Open areas nearby make it easier to find food.
fields.migration: It is usually present all year in its French breeding areas. Young birds can travel before settling down.
fields.by_ear: Its deep, ringing call sounds like a low croak. It also makes other sounds, sometimes surprisingly varied.
fields.confusions: The Carrion Crow is smaller and its tail looks less pointed in flight. The Northern Raven has a heavier bill.
fields.anecdote: Birds can roll over and play in the air currents.
fields.hint: My tail forms a wedge and my voice rings deep.

fields.summary: The Dunlin is a small mudflat bird with a slightly curved bill. In breeding plumage, it has a black patch on its belly.
fields.behaviour: It probes the mud or pecks to catch small animals. It often feeds in groups that move together.
fields.why_here: Mudflats uncovered by the tide are full of food. It also uses lagoons and other wetlands during its travels.
fields.migration: It is common in France during migration and winter. Birds can be seen at other times without breeding here.
fields.by_ear: Its contact calls are short, rolling and a little rasping. They often go with group take-offs.
fields.confusions: The Sanderling has a shorter, straighter bill. The Dunlin's black belly patch only shows in breeding plumage.
fields.anecdote: A flock can change direction all at once above the mud.
fields.hint: In summer, a black patch marks my belly.

fields.summary: The Green Sandpiper is a shorebird with a dark back and a white belly. When it takes off, its white rump stands out sharply against its dark wings.
fields.behaviour: It looks for small animals in shallow water. Often quiet and alone, it flies off suddenly when you come close.
fields.why_here: It uses ponds, ditches, muddy banks and small streams. Sheltered wetlands suit it well.
fields.migration: You can see it in France during migration and in winter. Seeing birds in different seasons does not mean each one stays in place.
fields.by_ear: Its whistled calls are loud and clear, often shouted as it flies away.
fields.confusions: The Wood Sandpiper has a stronger eyebrow and a pale underwing. The Green Sandpiper looks darker in flight.
fields.anecdote: In its breeding areas, it can use an old nest of another bird in a tree.
fields.hint: My white rump suddenly shows between two dark wings.

fields.summary: The Greylag Goose is a big grey goose with a thick, pale bill. Its noisy flocks visit wetlands and open country.
fields.behaviour: It grazes on grass and also eats seeds. Groups travel between their resting places on the water and their feeding areas.
fields.why_here: Lakes, marshes and meadows give it water to rest on and plants to eat.
fields.migration: Some birds stay all year in France. Migrants also arrive in the cold season, and the groups change from region to region.
fields.by_ear: Its powerful, nasal calls remind you of farmyard geese. Birds often answer each other in flight.
fields.confusions: The adult Greater White-fronted Goose has a white mark on the forehead and dark bars on the belly. The Greylag Goose does not have these marks.
fields.anecdote: It is the ancestor of many European farm goose breeds.
fields.hint: I graze in a flock and travel with loud calls.

fields.summary: The Common Snipe is a streaky brown bird with a very long, straight bill. Its feathers make it hard to see in wet grass.
fields.behaviour: It pushes its bill into soft ground to find small animals. When surprised, it often shoots up suddenly and zigzags away.
fields.why_here: Marshes, waterlogged meadows and muddy edges give it soft ground that is easy to probe.
fields.migration: It is in France in several seasons, mostly during migration and in winter. Breeding here is much more local.
fields.by_ear: In its display flight, the male makes a buzzing sound with his tail feathers. This noise is not a song from his throat.
fields.confusions: The Jack Snipe is smaller and its bill is shorter for its size. It often stays hidden until you are very close.
fields.anecdote: The trembling sound of its display comes from air passing over some tail feathers.
fields.hint: My very long bill explores the mud under the grass.

fields.summary: The male Eurasian Wigeon has a rusty head lit by a cream stripe on the forehead. The female has duller brown feathers.
fields.behaviour: It likes to graze on short grass near water. It also eats water plants and often feeds in groups.
fields.why_here: Coastal marshes, river mouths and wet meadows give it plants to eat and water to rest on.
fields.migration: You find it in France mostly in winter and during migration. A few sightings outside these times do not mean the same birds stay all year.
fields.by_ear: The male gives a clear whistle that carries far over the water. The female makes rougher sounds.
fields.confusions: The male Northern Pintail has a long white neck and a pointed tail. The Eurasian Wigeon looks more compact, with a pale stripe on the forehead.
fields.anecdote: You can see it grazing on land like a small goose.
fields.hint: My cream forehead goes with a whistle above the marsh.

fields.summary: The Common Redshank is a shorebird with red legs. Its bill is red at the base and dark at the tip.
fields.behaviour: It walks on mud and in shallow water to catch small animals. Near its nest, it can sound the alarm again and again.
fields.why_here: Marshes, wet meadows and mudflats give it food and resting places. It nests on the ground in plants.
fields.migration: Some birds nest in France, others pass through or spend the winter. So you can meet it all year in some wetlands.
fields.by_ear: It gives loud whistles, sometimes sad-sounding. Its calls become repeated and urgent when it sounds the alarm.
fields.confusions: The Spotted Redshank has a longer bill and a more slender look. In flight, the Common Redshank shows a wide white band at the back of the wings.
fields.anecdote: It can perch on a post to watch over the area around its nest.
fields.hint: I perch on a post to keep watch over my nest.

fields.summary: The Great Crested Grebe is a diving bird with a long neck. In the breeding season, its head has a dark crest and a rusty frill.
fields.behaviour: It dives to fish. Partners face each other and perform a display with head movements and sometimes water plants.
fields.why_here: Lakes and ponds give it fish. Plants on the shore can hold its floating nest.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in France. Some birds travel between breeding sites and big lakes or coasts used in winter.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are loud and varied, often rough. They can surprise you on a seemingly calm lake.
fields.confusions: The Little Grebe is much smaller and plumper. The Great Crested Grebe has a much longer neck.
fields.anecdote: The striped chicks can ride on an adult's back.
fields.hint: My striped chicks sometimes ride on my back.

fields.summary: The Western Cattle Egret is a small white heron with a fairly short neck. It often feeds on land, near herds.
fields.behaviour: It catches insects and other small prey stirred up by the passing animals. It can also follow farm machines.
fields.why_here: Meadows, pastures and crops give it food. It gathers in trees to sleep or nest.
fields.migration: It is present all year in several regions of France. Birds can still move around, especially depending on winter conditions.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are short, rough and not very musical. It is often silent when it hunts in a meadow.
fields.confusions: The Little Egret is slimmer, with a dark bill. The Western Cattle Egret usually has a yellow bill and a more hunched posture.
fields.anecdote: A passing cow can make its hunting easier by making insects move.
fields.hint: I use the herd's footsteps to find my meal.

fields.summary: The Green-winged Teal is a tiny duck. The male has a rusty head crossed by a wide green band around the eye.
fields.behaviour: It takes small seeds and water animals near the surface. Groups often rest close together on a bank.
fields.why_here: Marshes, shallow ponds and sheltered mudflats give it food and rest.
fields.migration: It is most numerous in France in the cold season. A small population also nests in the country, and migrants stop here.
fields.by_ear: The male gives a small, clear whistle. The female quacks more quietly than a big duck.
fields.confusions: The male Garganey has a big white eyebrow. Outside breeding plumage, you need to look more carefully at the wings and head.
fields.anecdote: Its small size lets it feed in very shallow water.
fields.hint: My tiny size lets me feed in very shallow water.

fields.summary: The Hen Harrier is a bird of prey with long wings. The adult male is pale grey, while the brown female has a very visible white rump.
fields.behaviour: It flies low to spot small mammals and birds. It can sleep on the ground in a shared roost.
fields.why_here: Heaths, marshes, wasteland and farm plains give it hunting grounds. It hides its nest in plants on the ground.
fields.migration: Some birds nest and stay in France, while others come for the winter. How many you see varies between regions and seasons.
fields.by_ear: Its calls are mostly heard near the nest or during encounters. When hunting in winter, it is often silent.
fields.confusions: The male Montagu's Harrier is slimmer and shows a black bar on the wing. Females and young birds are harder to tell apart.
fields.anecdote: Several birds can join the same roost in the grass at dusk.
fields.hint: My white rump marks my low passes over the moor.

fields.summary: The Common Shelduck is a big duck with very contrasting colors. Its red bill, dark head and wide rusty belt make it easy to know.
fields.behaviour: It strains mud and water to eat small animals. It often looks for food by walking in shallow water.
fields.why_here: River mouths, lagoons and coastal marshes give it food. It uses a hole to nest.
fields.migration: You find it all year in France, but birds can change region, especially to renew their feathers after breeding.
fields.by_ear: The male whistles, while the female makes lower, more nasal calls.
fields.confusions: Its white, black and rusty feathers and its red bill usually set it apart from other ducks seen in France.
fields.anecdote: It can make its nest in an old rabbit burrow.
fields.hint: My rusty belt separates a white chest from a dark neck.

fields.summary: The Common Pochard is a diving duck. The male combines a rusty head, a black chest and a pale grey back.
fields.behaviour: It dives to take plants and small water animals. It likes to rest in groups on open water.
fields.why_here: Ponds, lakes and old gravel pits give it places to dive. Plants on the shores can hide the nests.
fields.migration: It is present all year in France, with more birds in many areas in winter. Some come from regions further north or east.
fields.by_ear: It is usually quiet outside of displays. Females can make rough calls.
fields.confusions: The male Red-crested Pochard has a big orange head and a red bill. The Common Pochard has a dark bill with a paler patch.
fields.anecdote: To eat, it can disappear completely under the surface and come back up a little further away.
fields.hint: My rusty head sits above a black chest and a grey back.

fields.summary: The Northern Pintail is a slim duck with a long neck. In the male, the tail ends in long, pointed feathers.
fields.behaviour: It feeds near the surface or tips forward to reach plants and small water animals.
fields.why_here: Shallow marshes, flooded meadows and river mouths give it open feeding areas.
fields.migration: You see it in France mainly during migration and in winter. Sightings in other seasons are much rarer.
fields.by_ear: The male gives soft whistles. The female makes quiet quacks.
fields.confusions: The Mallard has a bulkier shape and a shorter neck. The male Northern Pintail shows a long white neck rising onto the brown head.
fields.anecdote: It can look for food with its head under water, keeping its tail up.
fields.hint: A long white neck rises onto my brown head.

fields.summary: The European Golden Plover is a bird of open country with a back finely speckled with gold. Its belly turns dark in breeding plumage.
fields.behaviour: It moves in short runs and pauses to take worms and other small animals. In winter, it sometimes gathers with lapwings.
fields.why_here: Short meadows, fields and plowed land give it wide spaces to feed and watch the surroundings.
fields.migration: It visits France mostly during migration and in winter. It goes back to breeding areas further north in spring.
fields.by_ear: Its call is a soft, clear, slightly sad whistle, given by birds on the ground or in flight.
fields.confusions: The Grey Plover shows black armpits in flight. The European Golden Plover has a paler underwing and a back with golden glints.
fields.anecdote: At rest, a flock can become almost invisible on an earth-colored field.
fields.hint: I rest in a flock, almost invisible on an earth-colored field.

fields.summary: The Northern Shoveler has a surprisingly wide bill at the tip. The male has a green head, a white chest and rusty sides.
fields.behaviour: It strains the water with its bill to catch small prey and edible bits. It often feeds while moving slowly forward.
fields.why_here: Marshes and shallow ponds give it water rich in food near the surface.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in France. Migration and winter bring extra birds, depending on the region.
fields.by_ear: It is often quiet. The male makes short, dull sounds, and the female quacks.
fields.confusions: The Mallard does not have a bill that is so wide at the end. This also helps you spot the brown females.
fields.anecdote: The edges of its bill have little plates that help filter food.
fields.hint: My wide bill turns water into a filtered meal.

fields.summary: The Tufted Duck is a diving duck with a yellow eye. The black male has white sides and a small crest behind the head.
fields.behaviour: It dives to catch small water animals, especially shellfish. It also eats plants.
fields.why_here: Lakes, ponds and gravel pits give it waters to dive in. Plants on the banks can hide the nests.
fields.migration: It is present all year in France, but many sites hold more birds in winter. Groups move around depending on conditions.
fields.by_ear: It is often silent in its wintering places. Quiet calls go with encounters between birds.
fields.confusions: The male Greater Scaup has a grey back and no crest. The male Tufted Duck has a black back.
fields.anecdote: The male's little crest changes look with his posture and the wind.
fields.hint: My yellow eyes shine above white flanks.

fields.summary: The Ruff is a long-legged shorebird. In display season, males can wear a spectacular collar of feathers.
fields.behaviour: It looks for seeds and small animals in wetlands. At displays, males gather and spread their showy feathers.
fields.why_here: Flooded meadows, marshes and mudflats give it places to feed and rest.
fields.migration: It crosses France during migration and some birds spend the winter here. It usually breeds further north and east.
fields.by_ear: It is usually quiet and makes little sound apart from close encounters.
fields.confusions: Females and young birds can look like other shorebirds. Differences in size between birds and the fairly short bill are clues to combine with others.
fields.anecdote: Not all males have a collar of the same color.
fields.hint: At display time, males gather to show off their finery.

fields.summary: The Black-crowned Night Heron is a stocky heron with red eyes. The adult has a dark back and cap, with grey wings.
fields.behaviour: It often hunts at dusk and at night. Standing still near the water, it waits for fish and other small prey.
fields.why_here: Rivers, ponds and marshes give it fishing spots. Nearby trees or bushes shelter its resting places and colonies.
fields.migration: You see it mostly in the warm season in France, but some birds also spend the winter. Part of the birds migrate to Africa.
fields.by_ear: Its flight call is rough and short. You can hear it at night before you see its shape.
fields.confusions: The young bird, brown with pale spots, looks very different from the adult. The Grey Heron is bigger and more slender.
fields.anecdote: A bird hidden in a tree during the day can go off hunting when night falls.
fields.hint: My red eyes keep watch near the water at dusk.

fields.summary: The Little Gull is a very small gull. In adults, the dark underside of the wings contrasts with their pale edge.
fields.behaviour: It catches insects in flight and takes small prey from the water's surface. It sometimes feeds in groups.
fields.why_here: Lakes, lagoons, river mouths and coastal waters give it food-rich stops or winter homes.
fields.migration: It crosses France and also visits its waters in winter. Sightings in different seasons are not always the same birds.
fields.by_ear: Its small calls are fairly quiet. Its shape and wing pattern are usually more useful to identify it.
fields.confusions: The Black-headed Gull is bigger and does not have the adult's dark underwing. Young birds need careful watching.
fields.anecdote: The feathers on its wings change a lot between the first years and adulthood.
fields.hint: As an adult, I show the dark underside of my wings.

fields.summary: The Little Stint is a tiny shorebird with a short bill. It trots over the mud to take very small prey.
fields.behaviour: It pecks quickly at the wet surface. It can mix with other small mudflat birds during its stops.
fields.why_here: Pond edges, lagoons and mudflats give it open surfaces full of tiny animals.
fields.migration: You see it in France mainly during migration. Some birds also stay for the winter, especially in good wetlands.
fields.by_ear: It gives thin, short calls, easy to miss in a group of noisier birds.
fields.confusions: The Dunlin is bigger and has a longer, slightly curved bill. Other very small sandpipers need a careful look.
fields.anecdote: Its tiny size is easy to spot when it feeds next to other shorebirds.
fields.hint: I trot over the mud with a short bill.

fields.summary: The Eurasian Woodcock is a forest bird with a long bill. Its brown feathers with dark marks hide it among dead leaves.
fields.behaviour: It probes soft ground to find worms and other small animals. It can leave the woods at night to feed in meadows.
fields.why_here: Woods with soft, food-rich ground suit it. Nearby edges and meadows add more feeding places.
fields.migration: Some birds nest in France. Others arrive for the winter, then go back to their breeding areas in spring.
fields.by_ear: During its display flight, the male alternates low sounds and a high call. You hear him mostly at dusk.
fields.confusions: The Common Snipe is slimmer and lives mostly in open wetlands. The Eurasian Woodcock is plumper and tied to woods.
fields.anecdote: Its eyes, set high on its head, give it a wide view while it digs in the ground.
fields.hint: My feathers look like dead leaves on the forest floor.

fields.summary: The Great Egret is a big, all-white heron with a very long neck. It fishes by walking slowly or standing still.
fields.behaviour: It catches fish, amphibians and other small animals. In meadows, it can also hunt small mammals.
fields.why_here: Marshes, ponds, rivers and wet meadows give it hunting grounds. It nests in reedbeds or trees, depending on the site.
fields.migration: You can see it all year in France. Birds move between breeding sites, dispersal areas and winter homes.
fields.by_ear: It is often silent when hunting. Its calls are rough, mostly when disturbed or when talking at the colony.
fields.confusions: The Little Egret is smaller and usually has yellow feet. The Great Egret has an especially long neck and a more imposing shape.
fields.anecdote: Like other herons, it folds its neck back in flight.
fields.hint: All white, I fold my long neck to fly.

fields.summary: The Eurasian Curlew is a big shorebird with a very long bill curving downward. Its brown feathers are finely streaked.
fields.behaviour: It uses its bill to grab prey from the ground or the mud. It eats worms, crustaceans and insects, among other things.
fields.why_here: Mudflats, marshes and meadows give it food. Nesting birds look for open spaces with plants right for a ground nest.
fields.migration: Some birds nest in France, while others pass through or spend the winter. Some coasts have them in several seasons.
fields.by_ear: Its call is loud and flute-like. It can sound like its name, with a note that rises and then stretches out.
fields.confusions: The Whimbrel has a shorter bill and strong dark stripes on the head. The Eurasian Curlew usually looks bigger.
fields.anecdote: Bill length varies between birds, and females often have the longer bill.
